title: A film is still frames shown fast
description: A film is a series of still photographs projected in rapid succession, fast enough to look like smooth movement.

facts.text: Britannica defines a film as a series of still photographs projected onto a screen in rapid succession, giving the illusion of smooth, continuous movement.

title: From photographs to projection to television
description: Moving pictures grew from sequence photographs (1878) to films projected for a paying audience (1895), then to television, which delivers moving images electronically.

facts.text: In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge photographed a galloping horse with a row of cameras, a step from still photography toward motion pictures.
On December 28, 1895, the Lumière brothers projected films for a paying audience at the Grand Café in Paris.
Television delivers moving images and sound electronically from a source to a receiver; in 1928 General Electric began regular experimental television broadcasts in the United States.

title: The crafts that make a film
description: Film draws on nearly every other art plus technical skills: screenwriting, directing, acting, cinematography, design, music, sound and editing.

facts.text: Film requires contributions from nearly all the other arts as well as countless technical skills, such as sound recording, photography and optics.
Film developed as a means of artistic expression in acting, directing, screenwriting, cinematography, costume and set design, and music.
Editing is trimming and piecing together lengths of film into a complete motion picture; the editor judges how long each shot should last.

title: Apparent motion: the brain supplies the movement
description: Wertheimer's phi phenomenon and beta movement show the brain sees motion between still images shown in quick succession; to the visual system, film motion is like real motion.

facts.text: Psychologist Max Wertheimer described the phi phenomenon in 1912; he reportedly noticed it in 1910 when two alternating railway signal lights looked like one light in motion.
Beta movement occurs when a series of still images shows an object in a slightly different position in each image, and viewers see the object move.
The phi phenomenon and beta movement explain how animation, film and electronic displays create the illusion of continuous motion from a sequence of still images.
The visual system seemingly cannot tell the short-range apparent motion in a motion picture from real motion.

title: Persistence of vision: the older, oversimplified story
description: The claim that images linger on the retina and blend is an inadequate explanation of film motion; researchers separate flicker fusion from apparent motion.

facts.text: Persistence of vision, the idea that each image lingers on the retina and blends with the next, recurred in film writing for almost a century but is an inadequate explanation of apparent motion; blended images would only superimpose.
Perceptual psychology separates two effects in film: flicker fusion, which makes flickering light look steady, and apparent motion, which makes successive images look like movement.

title: Frame rates, from hand cranks to 24
description: A frame rate counts frames per second. The brain needs more than about 15; silent cameras were hand-cranked at 16 to 18 on average, and sound fixed the standard at 24 in 1927.

facts.text: The brain perceives continuous movement from a succession of still images exposed at a rate above 15 frames per second.
Silent-film cameras were mainly hand-cranked, at rates averaging 16 to 18 frames per second.
Silent films were photographed and projected at widely varying speeds.
Sound made a standard frame rate necessary, and in 1927 the speed was standardized at 24 frames per second, or 90 feet per minute for 35 mm film.
Cameras were motorized in 1929 to run at an even speed of 24 frames per second so sound stayed in sync.

title: Shooting speed versus showing speed
description: Film must be projected at the speed it was shot; project it faster and the action speeds up, shoot it faster and it plays in slow motion.

facts.text: To look natural, film must be projected at the speed it was shot: action filmed at 12 frames per second and projected at 24 plays twice as fast, and action filmed at 36 or more frames per second looks slow at 24.

title: Muybridge's galloping horse
description: Hired by Leland Stanford, Muybridge used a row of 12 thread-triggered cameras in 1878 to show a galloping horse lifts all four hooves at once, legs tucked under.

facts.text: Railroad magnate Leland Stanford hired photographer Eadweard Muybridge to prove that at one moment in its gallop a horse has all four legs off the ground.
On June 19, 1878, at Stanford's Palo Alto track, Muybridge photographed the mare Sallie Gardner galloping past a row of 12 cameras.
The camera shutters were released as the horse broke threads attached to them.
The photos showed a galloping horse with all four hooves off the ground at once, legs tucked under its body, not stretched out front and back as painters had shown.

title: The zoopraxiscope: photos projected in motion
description: Muybridge's zoopraxiscope projected his sequence images in rapid succession, a predecessor of cinema, but each sequence needed many cameras.

facts.text: Muybridge developed the zoopraxiscope, a lantern that projected images in rapid succession onto a screen and an important predecessor of cinema.

Muybridge's projected sequences came from multiple cameras; a camera invented in Edison's lab that recorded successive images by itself was more practical and influenced all later motion picture devices.

title: The Kinetoscope, a one-viewer movie cabinet
description: Developed largely by W. K. L. Dickson in Edison's lab, the Kinetoscope let one person at a time watch a film loop through a peephole; the first parlor opened in New York on April 14, 1894.

facts.text: In February 1888 Muybridge visited Edison's laboratory in West Orange, New Jersey, and proposed combining the zoopraxiscope with the phonograph; Edison did not join him.
In October 1888 Edison filed a caveat for a device to "do for the eye what the phonograph does for the ear", which he called the Kinetoscope.
Edison's assistant W. K. L. Dickson, given the task in 1889, did the bulk of the experimenting, and most modern scholars give him the major credit, though Edison took sole credit.

The Kinetoscope was a wooden cabinet about four feet high; one viewer looked through a peephole at a loop of film about 50 feet long, drawn continuously past a lamp while a spinning shutter let through very brief flashes.
The first Kinetoscope parlor opened in New York on April 14, 1894, with five machines in a row; 25 cents let a customer watch the film in each.

title: Why projection beat the peep show
description: Projecting for a crowd earned more per machine than one-viewer cabinets, so projection overtook the Kinetoscope from 1895; Edison sold Armat and Jenkins's Vitascope as his own in 1896.

facts.text: Edison was slow to develop projection because Kinetoscopes were very profitable, but films projected for large audiences could earn more because fewer machines were needed for the number of viewers.
Projected motion pictures began to overtake Kinetoscope peep shows in 1895.
The Vitascope projector, invented by Thomas Armat and C. Francis Jenkins but marketed as an Edison invention, had its first theatrical showing in New York on April 23, 1896.

title: The Lumières' 1895 Paris screening
description: On December 28, 1895, the Lumières projected short everyday-life films for a paying audience at the Grand Café in Paris, usually counted as cinema's birth; their light three-in-one Cinématographe traveled the world.

facts.text: On December 28, 1895, the Lumière brothers held a showing at the Grand Café on the boulevard des Capucines in Paris, which Britannica calls the beginning of cinema history.
Before the commercial premiere of December 28, 1895, the Lumières had shown their Cinématographe at demonstrations, the first for a small audience in Paris on March 22, 1895.
Woodville Latham's Eidoloscope projector was presented publicly in New York in April 1895.
The Lumières' work began after their father, Antoine, saw Edison's Kinetoscope in Paris in 1894; they aimed to show moving pictures to an audience rather than to one viewer at a time.
The Cinématographe weighed under 5 kg and combined the jobs of camera, printer and projector, which made it easy for operators to travel.
The Lumières' first films recorded everyday French life, such as workers leaving the Lumière factory and a train arriving at a station.
Beginning in 1896 the Lumières sent trained cameraman-projectionists to cities around the world to show films and shoot new ones.

title: The train panic is a legend
description: No reports from the time show audiences fleeing the Lumières' arriving-train film; historian Martin Loiperdinger calls the tale cinema's founding myth.

facts.text: The story that audiences panicked at the Lumières' film of an arriving train has no support in reports from the time; historian Martin Loiperdinger calls the panic legend cinema's founding myth.

title: Méliès and the stop trick
description: Stage magician Georges Méliès saw the Lumière show and turned the camera into a magic box, using the stop trick (stop, change the scene, restart), which Edison's company had used in 1895.

facts.text: Georges Méliès, a stage magician, owned the Théâtre Robert-Houdin in Paris from 1888.
In December 1895, Méliès, then running the Théâtre Robert-Houdin, saw the Lumière Cinématographe demonstrated in Paris.
By Méliès's own account, his camera jammed while he was filming in the Place de l'Opéra, and when he projected the film a bus seemed to turn into a hearse: the stop trick, or substitution splice.
Edison's company had already used the trick in 1895: filming The Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, it stopped the camera, replaced the actor with a dummy, and resumed filming.
Méliès's films used stop motion, slow motion, dissolves, fade-outs, superimposition and double exposure.
Méliès built a glass-walled film studio at Montreuil, near Paris.

title: A Trip to the Moon
description: Méliès's 1902 A Trip to the Moon, loosely from Jules Verne, used stop motion and superimposition, reached audiences internationally and helped make story films mainstream.

facts.text: A Trip to the Moon (1902), loosely adapted from Jules Verne, runs about 14 minutes and includes the spacecraft striking the man in the moon in the eye.
In A Trip to the Moon, Méliès used camera tricks such as stop motion and superimposition to create fantasy.
A Trip to the Moon was one of the first films to achieve international distribution and helped establish story films as a mainstream product.

title: The Great Train Robbery tells a story across places
description: Porter's 1903 film for Edison's company used 14 shots and cut between the telegraph operator and the bandits to show simultaneous action, a break from theater-like staging.

facts.text: The Great Train Robbery (1903) was made by Edwin S. Porter for Thomas Edison's company and runs about 12 minutes.
The film is built from 14 separate shots: bandits overpower a telegraph operator, rob a train's mail car and passengers, and are chased by a posse.
Porter cut back and forth between the tied-up telegraph operator and the bandits on the train to show action happening at the same time in different places.
Britannica describes the film as a dramatic departure from the front-facing, theatrical staging of its day, establishing continuity of action from shot to shot.

title: The Great Train Robbery on location and on screen
description: Shot in November 1903 in Edison's New York studio and on location in New Jersey, the film ends or opens with an outlaw firing at the camera and helped make the Western a staple.

facts.text: The Great Train Robbery was filmed in November 1903 at Edison's New York studio and on location in New Jersey, including along the Lackawanna Railroad.
In a close-up, the outlaw leader, played by Justus D. Barnes, fires his pistol straight at the camera; exhibitors could show it at the beginning or the end of the film.
The film's success tapped into fascination with the Old West and helped make the Western a staple of American film.

title: Intermittent movement: stop, show, pull
description: A projector advances film one frame at a time and holds each frame still while it is shown; claws or a Maltese cross do the pulling.

facts.text: Intermittent movement advances film one frame at a time, with stationary periods in between, so each frame stands still while it is exposed or shown.
In cameras, the intermittent is typically a claw mechanism that pulls the film down by its sprocket holes.
The four-slot Maltese cross, or Geneva movement, introduced in the 1890s, stops each frame of the moving film in front of the projector's picture aperture.
The Lumière Cinématographe worked like a sewing machine, moving film then holding it still: a cam drove claws through the film's perforations, and two turns of the crank a second advanced 16 frames.

title: The shutter hides the pull and beats flicker
description: A rotating shutter blocks the light while each frame is pulled down, and a twin-bladed shutter flashes each frame twice (48 flashes at 24 fps) to prevent flicker.

facts.text: A rotating shutter blocks the light while the film is pulled down to the next frame, so the movement is never seen.
Flicker happens when images are not flashed quickly enough for the viewer to see the light as continuously on.
Film projectors generally use a twin-bladed shutter that flashes each frame twice, so a film shown at 24 frames per second gives 48 flashes per second.

title: Films saved as paper prints
description: To register copyright, Edison's company and others deposited films at the Library of Congress as photographic prints on paper, which now form its Paper Print Collection.

facts.text: Film companies often copied each other's films, so from October 1896 the Edison Company regularly registered films for copyright, sending them to the Library of Congress as positive photographic prints on paper rolls.
These paper prints, with those from other companies, form the Library of Congress's Paper Print Collection.
The earliest surviving copyrighted film, Edison Kinetoscopic Record of a Sneeze, January 7, 1894, was deposited as a series of photographic prints, not on film.
The Library of Congress holds The Great Train Robbery in its Paper Print Collection.

title: The nickelodeon boom
description: Cheap storefront theaters, named for their nickel admission, spread from Pittsburgh in 1905 to thousands by 1908 and made movies everyday entertainment.

facts.text: A nickelodeon was an early movie theater named for its nickel admission; it showed short films continuously, with piano accompaniment.
Harry Davis's Pittsburgh nickelodeon, opened in 1905, became the model for the rapid spread of nickelodeons across the United States.
Nickelodeons were makeshift theaters in converted storefronts, showing about an hour's worth of films for 5 to 10 cents.
Britannica credits the popularity of The Great Train Robbery with encouraging investors and leading to the first permanent film theaters, the nickelodeons.
The number of nickelodeons in the United States grew from a handful in 1904 to between 8,000 and 10,000 by 1908.
Nickelodeons were first identified with working-class audiences, drew more middle-class viewers as the decade went on, and became tied to the rising popularity of the story film.

title: Film exchanges: renting instead of buying
description: Instead of buying prints outright, theaters rented them from film exchanges, which bought prints from producers and leased them cheaply.

facts.text: From about 1897 producers sold film prints outright to exhibitors.
Around 1903 Harry and Herbert Miles opened a film exchange in San Francisco that bought prints from producers and leased them to exhibitors for 25 percent of the purchase price.

title: The Trust: the Motion Picture Patents Company
description: In 1908 leading film companies, Edison's among them, pooled their patents in the Motion Picture Patents Company and licensed who could make and show films.

facts.text: In 1908 leading film companies, including Edison's and Biograph, formed the Motion Picture Patents Company, known as the Trust, pooling the key US film patents.
The Trust licensed its patents only to approved companies and had an exclusive deal with Eastman Kodak, so raw film stock went only to licensed producers.
The US government sued the Motion Picture Patents Company under the Sherman Antitrust Act, and the company was formally dissolved in 1918.

title: Why filmmaking moved to Hollywood
description: Southern California offered year-round sun, varied scenery and cheap land and labor, and distance from the Trust is generally thought to have helped; by 1915 Hollywood was the center of US filmmaking.

facts.text: In 1911 a site on Sunset Boulevard became Hollywood's first studio, and soon about 20 companies were producing films in the area.
By 1915 Hollywood had become the center of the American film industry as independent filmmakers moved there from the East Coast, with more than 60 percent of American production based there.
Southern California offered a temperate climate for year-round filming, a wide range of scenery within 50 miles of Hollywood, low taxes, and cheap, plentiful labor and land.
It is generally thought that Hollywood's distance from the Motion Picture Patents Company's headquarters in New York City made it attractive to independent filmmakers.

title: Alice Guy's early story films
description: Alice Guy, Léon Gaumont's secretary, directed La Fée aux choux, one of the first films to tell a made-up story, and went on to run Gaumont's production.

facts.text: Hired as Léon Gaumont's secretary, Alice Guy directed her first film, La Fée aux choux (The Cabbage Fairy), which Britannica dates to 1896; a few historians date it as late as 1900.
Britannica says Guy is generally acknowledged to be the first director to film a narrative story, and many historians hold that her fairy tale preceded Méliès's story films.
Guy became the Gaumont company's head of production, directing nearly all Gaumont films made until 1905.
From 1906 to 1907 Guy directed short sound films using Gaumont's Chronophone.

title: Alice Guy's American studio and lost credit
description: Guy moved to the United States in 1907, founded Solax in 1910 and built a Fort Lee studio, yet many of her achievements were later forgotten or credited to men.

facts.text: In 1907 Guy married cameraman Herbert Blaché and moved to the United States, where in 1910 she founded the Solax Company.
By 1912 Solax had a new, state-of-the-art studio in Fort Lee, New Jersey.
Many of Guy's accomplishments were forgotten or credited to male colleagues, and after returning to France in 1922 she could not find work in its film industry.

title: Griffith's techniques and the feature film
description: D. W. Griffith refined the close-up and cross-cutting over hundreds of Biograph shorts, and his nearly three-hour The Birth of a Nation secured the feature-length film.

facts.text: From 1908 to 1913 D. W. Griffith made more than 400 films for Biograph, mostly one-reelers.
Britannica says Griffith introduced or refined techniques of film storytelling, including the close-up and cross-cutting, which edits together scenes at different locations.
The Birth of a Nation (1915), based on Thomas Dixon's 1905 novel The Clansman, ran nearly three hours, one of the longest films made up to that time.
The Birth of a Nation used special effects, jump cuts and facial close-ups, and Britannica says it secured the future of feature-length films and the acceptance of film as a serious medium.

title: The racism of The Birth of a Nation and the protests against it
description: The Birth of a Nation portrayed Black people as unworthy of freedom and glorified the Ku Klux Klan; the NAACP led protests, and the film inspired the Klan's 1915 revival.

facts.text: The Birth of a Nation portrays Black people during Reconstruction as unworthy of freedom and voting rights, and shows the Ku Klux Klan as heroes restoring order.
In The Birth of a Nation, Black characters such as Gus were played by white actors in blackface.
Protests, mainly organized by the NAACP, met The Birth of a Nation from its 1915 premiere, and showings were stopped in a few states and cities.
In late 1915 the Ku Klux Klan was revived in Georgia, directly inspired by The Birth of a Nation.
Griffith responded to criticism of The Birth of a Nation with Intolerance (1916), a film about intolerance and censorship.

title: Chaplin's Tramp
description: Charlie Chaplin's Tramp, first seen in 1914, mixed physical comedy with poignancy; Chaplin directed his own films and cofounded United Artists.

facts.text: While touring America with the Karno company in 1913, Charlie Chaplin was signed to appear in Mack Sennett's Keystone comedies.
Chaplin's Tramp first appeared in Kid Auto Races at Venice (1914), wearing a too-small coat, too-large pants, floppy shoes and a battered derby, with a small mustache and a cane.
Chaplin blended physical comedy with poignancy; in The Gold Rush (1925) the Tramp must eat his shoe to stay alive.
Chaplin became his own director, and in 1919 he cofounded United Artists with Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and D. W. Griffith.

title: Keaton's deadpan stunts
description: Buster Keaton, the Great Stone Face, did dangerous stunts with an unsmiling face, timed to the inch, as in the falling house front of Steamboat Bill, Jr.

facts.text: In Steamboat Bill, Jr. (1928), a house front falls on Buster Keaton, who survives by standing on a nail-marked spot where its open attic window lands; had he moved, he would have been crushed.
Keaton grew up in his family's vaudeville act, the Three Keatons, known for knockabout acrobatics, and learned to take pratfalls without injury.
Buster Keaton, known as the Great Stone Face, performed death-defying stunts while keeping an unsmiling expression.
Keaton said that the more serious he turned, the bigger the laugh he could get.
In The General, a Civil War comedy, Keaton staged most of the action and stunts in and around trains.

title: Intertitles
description: Silent films cut to printed cards, intertitles, for dialogue or explanation; a few films, like The Last Laugh, managed almost without them.

facts.text: Silent films used printed intertitles for dialogue or explanation.
F. W. Murnau's Der letzte Mann (The Last Laugh, 1924) told its story almost entirely without printed intertitles.

title: Live music at the silent movies
description: Silent films were almost always shown with live music: an improvising pianist at first, organs and orchestras in big theaters, guided by cue sheets and compiled scores.

facts.text: Silent films were almost always shown with live music: early screenings usually had a solo pianist, often improvising, and larger theaters used organists or orchestras.
Films were eventually distributed with published cue sheets suggesting what the pianist or organist should play.
The Birth of a Nation was shown with an orchestra playing Joseph Carl Breil's score, a compilation drawn from many sources.

title: Movie palaces
description: From 1914, huge, luxurious 'dream palaces' such as New York's Strand gave films grand theaters with thousands of seats.

facts.text: New York's Strand Theatre, opened in 1914, was the first of the 'dream palaces', huge movie theaters with luxurious interiors, and seated around 3,000 people.

title: Caligari's sets show a state of mind
description: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari used distorted sets and painted light and shadow to show a narrator's tortured mind.

facts.text: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, directed by Robert Wiene in postwar Germany, tells of murders committed by a sleepwalker at the bidding of a demented showman.
To represent the narrator's tortured state of mind, Wiene hired three Expressionist artists to design sets with exaggerated dimensions and deformed spatial relationships.
Patterns of light and shadow were painted directly onto Caligari's scenery and even the characters' makeup, partly to save electric power, which was rationed in postwar Germany.

title: German Expressionism
description: Caligari's success gave rise to German Expressionism, a movement of stylized, shadowy films including Murnau's Nosferatu.

facts.text: By embodying disturbed psychological states through décor, Caligari greatly influenced the UFA films that followed and gave rise to the movement known as German Expressionism.
F. W. Murnau directed one of the movement's classics, Nosferatu (1922), an unauthorized adaptation of Bram Stoker's novel Dracula.

title: Soviet cinema learns to edit
description: Lenin's government made film a priority and founded the world's first film school; short of film stock, teachers such as Kuleshov studied how Griffith's shots were assembled.

facts.text: Lenin recognized film's importance as propaganda and its power to communicate quickly, and his government gave top priority to developing the Soviet film industry.
The Soviet state film school in Moscow, later known as VGIK, was the first film school in the world.
A foreign blockade stopped the Soviet Union importing film equipment and stock, which it could not yet make itself, and power shortages limited what remained.
Teacher Lev Kuleshov screened a print of Griffith's Intolerance for his workshop students until they had memorized its shot structures.
Soviet filmmakers held that time and space in film must be subordinate to editing, which they called montage, from the French verb monter, 'to assemble'.

title: Eisenstein's montage of collision
description: Sergei Eisenstein held that meaning comes from the collision of opposing shots, and put the idea to work in the Odessa Steps sequence of Battleship Potemkin (1925).

facts.text: Eisenstein believed that meaning in film is generated by the collision of opposing shots, producing a new idea, and compared the process to the explosions of an internal combustion engine.
Battleship Potemkin (1925), commissioned for the 20th anniversary of the 1905 Revolution, dramatizes a mutiny by the sailors of the battleship Potemkin.
Potemkin's 'Odessa Steps' sequence, in which soldiers massacre citizens on a stone staircase, is one of the most famous sequences in film history, and montage gives the slaughter symbolic meaning.

title: What Nanook of the North staged
description: Nanook of the North filmed real Inuit people and skills, but arranged much for the camera: a cut-away igloo, a staged seal hunt, a borrowed family and harpoons instead of rifles.

facts.text: Robert Flaherty's Nanook of the North (1922), a dramatic interpretation of Inuit life in the Canadian Arctic, was an international success.
Flaherty arrived at Port Harrison (now Inukjuak) in northern Quebec in August 1920 to shoot the film; Allakariallak, chosen as the best hunter in the district, played Nanook.
To film inside an igloo, a second igloo was built with a wall removed to make room for the camera and its operator.
The two women shown as Nanook's wives were not his wives, and the two children were not his.
Nanook's famous seal hunt was staged, as close viewing of the cuts shows.
By 1920 Inuit hunters used rifles, but Flaherty had his subjects hunt with harpoons and spears to show an older way of life.

title: Flaherty and the word documentary
description: Flaherty is often called the father of the documentary film, and John Grierson first used the word documentary about Flaherty's Moana (1926).

facts.text: Robert Flaherty is often called the father of the documentary film.
John Grierson first used the term documentary in a reference to Flaherty's film Moana (1926).

title: Most American silent features are lost
description: A 2013 Library of Congress study found only 14 percent of 1912-1929 US features survive complete in their original form; nitrate decay, fire and neglect after sound destroyed most of the rest.

facts.text: A 2013 study by historian David Pierce for the Library of Congress found that only 14 percent of US feature films from 1912 to 1929 survive complete on 35mm as released; another 11 percent survive in foreign versions or lesser formats.
Derived from the 2013 study: with 14 percent of 1912-1929 US features surviving in original form and 11 percent in other versions, about three in four are lost.
The losses are blamed on nitrate film's vulnerability to fire and decay and the film industry's practice of neglecting or destroying prints and negatives.
Silent feature films disappeared from sight soon after the coming of sound, and many vanished from existence.

title: The five stages of making a film
description: A film moves through development, pre-production, production (the shoot) and post-production, then distribution brings it to audiences.

facts.text: Britannica describes the film value chain as running from the selection of an idea that could become a film to the film's consumption in a movie theater or on television.

Film production is usually composed of four phases: development, preproduction, filming and postproduction; the finished master copy is then sold to a distributor, which makes copies for theatrical release.

In development, a producer picks an original idea or buys the rights to an existing story, such as a novel, a comic book, a play or a game, has a writer develop a screenplay, estimates the costs and looks for money.
Preproduction work includes developing the script, auditioning the actors and planning how each scene will be shot.
The shooting phase usually lasts a few weeks and is delicate and expensive, because it involves the simultaneous work of several people.

title: Post-production turns footage into a finished film
description: Post-production usually lasts longer than the shoot: picture and sound are edited, effects, titles, music and sound effects are added, and everything is combined.

facts.text: The postproduction stage is likely to last longer than the shooting itself; picture and sound are edited, effects and titles are created, music and sound effects are added, and all are combined.

title: How a screenplay is laid out
description: A screenplay is the written basis of a film; each scene opens with a capitalized scene heading (INT. or EXT., place, time of day), followed by action lines and dialogue under capitalized character names.

facts.text: Britannica defines a screenplay as the written text that provides the basis for a film production.
In the Academy Nicholl Fellowships format guide, a scene heading, or slug line, is always in capitals and usually begins with INT. or EXT.; character names above dialogue are also in capitals.

A scene heading tells whether the scene is inside or outside, where it takes place and the time of day; action lines describe what the audience will see, and each speaker's name is in capitals with the dialogue below.

title: One screenplay page is about one minute
description: Because screenplays share one standard format (Courier, fixed margins), one page works out to about a minute of screen time, a rule of thumb used to estimate running time, budgets and schedules.

facts.text: Syd Field wrote that one page of screenplay is approximately one minute of screen time, whether the script is all action, all dialogue or a mix, and called it a good rule of thumb.
The Academy Nicholl Fellowships format guide calls Courier, 12-point, 10-pitch, the industry standard font for screenplays and advises against other fonts.

The page-per-minute estimate grew from the typewriter-era standard format: Courier, whose characters each take the same space, with standardized margins and spacing; studios use it to estimate budgets and shooting schedules.
One page per minute is only an estimate: a short action description can play for minutes on screen, while rapid-fire dialogue often runs faster than a minute a page.

title: Storyboards: the film drawn shot by shot
description: A storyboard is a shot-by-shot visual plan of a film, one panel per camera shot; the Disney studio pioneered it, and simple sketches are enough.

facts.text: ACMI, a museum of screen culture in Melbourne, describes a storyboard as a shot-by-shot visual plan that shows what a film will look like before it is shot; each panel represents a camera shot, and it guides the team shooting the film.
A storyboard does not recreate every frame of a film and need not be a work of art: simple sketches with stick figures can show the shot type and what is in the shot.
The Walt Disney Family Museum says the Walt Disney Studios pioneered storyboarding.
A storyboard is a series of sketches that maps out a story, letting filmmakers see the plot in sequence, judge whether the story is clear and spot plot holes or inconsistencies.

title: The shot list: every shot to capture
description: A shot list keeps track of every planned shot and its details, such as camera movement, so the crew knows what to film on the day.

facts.text: A shot list keeps track of all the shots so that, when filming comes, the crew knows what it needs to film; on set, filmmakers often keep the storyboard and script on hand to set up shots as planned.
A shot list can list each shot's camera movement; 'static' in that column means the camera should not move.

title: Producer and director
description: The producer manages a film's money and schedule from financing to final approval; the director develops the artistic vision and oversees each scene.

facts.text: Producers are a film's managers, from securing the financing in preproduction to approving the completed film; they hire the director, create the budget and approve changes to the script, budget or schedule.
The director develops and implements the film's artistic vision: helping choose the cast, overseeing the shooting of each scene, working closely with the cinematographer and guiding the actors.

title: Cinematographer, gaffer and grip
description: The cinematographer (director of photography) shoots the scenes and decides camera moves, lenses and lighting; the gaffer designs the lighting scheme; grips carry out the lighting plan and support the camera.

facts.text: The cinematographer, also called the director of photography, is in charge of shooting the scenes and decides how the camera should move to meet the director's vision.
A cinematographer chooses the camera and lenses to use and how to light each scene, and works closely with the director on setting up shots.

Gaffers supervise the electricians on a film set and design and adjust the lighting scheme for each scene; if a scene needs a campfire that can't be built on set, gaffers use lights to recreate its flicker.
The AFI's glossary defines the gaffer as the chief electrician on a film or television set.
Grips carry out the gaffer's lighting plan and may support the camera operator when the camera is rigged on a dolly or crane; the key grip oversees the other grips.

title: The script supervisor keeps continuity
description: The script supervisor records what was shot and how, take by take, so the footage cuts together seamlessly.

facts.text: A script supervisor records slate numbers, notes on each take, lenses, the action and running times, plus details of props, makeup and costume, so that the footage shot will cut together seamlessly.
The BFI describes film continuity as something that, by its nature, should be entirely invisible.

title: Shot sizes: wide, medium and close-up
description: Shots are named by how close the camera is to the subject: a wide (long) shot shows the whole body and setting, a medium shot roughly the waist up, a close-up the head.

facts.text: A shot type is defined by how close the camera is to the subject being filmed, which is usually a character but can be a setting or an object.
In a wide shot or long shot you see a character's whole body from head to toe, sometimes small within the landscape or space around them.
A medium shot, or mid shot, generally shows a character from roughly the waist up and is good for showing body language and a character performing actions.
In a close-up a person's head fills the frame; close-ups are good for showing emotion on characters' faces.
Shot scales are not universal: whether a shot counts as a close-up is judged in relation to the other shots in the same film.

title: What each shot size is for
description: Wide shots establish where a scene is and keep full-body action in view; close-ups draw viewers into a character's emotion.

facts.text: Establishing shots show the audience where a scene takes place and are usually long shots; extreme long shots are usually the first or last shots of a sequence.
Because a long shot can show a whole body moving without reframing, it is common in genres where full-body action must be seen, such as Hollywood musicals and 1970s martial arts films.
If a director wants the audience more emotionally involved in a key scene, the cinematographer might shoot the actors' faces at close range to capture their expressions.
A close-up can capture subtle emotion, such as a character trying hard to hide their feelings, not only extreme emotions like crying or fear.

title: Camera angles: eye level, low and high
description: Most shots are at eye level; a low angle looks up and can make a character seem strong or menacing, a high angle looks down and can make them seem small or weak.

facts.text: Eye level is the most standard camera angle; a large share of shots are taken from eye level because it is easy and natural for viewers.
In a low-angle shot the camera is placed well below eye level, facing up; it can make a character look heroic and strong, or a villain scary and intimidating.
In a high-angle shot the camera is above the character, angled down; it can make characters look small and weak.

In The Color of Paradise (1999), Majid Majidi's Iranian film, the father who rules his family is often shot from a low angle, and his blind son Mohammad and elderly grandmother from a high angle, stressing their dependence and smallness.
Readings of camera angles are not fixed: in The Color of Paradise, the high-angle view of Mohammad and his grandmother may also suggest that God is watching over them.

title: The Dutch (canted) angle
description: Tilting the camera so the frame is not level creates a sense of chaos, instability or unease.

facts.text: In a canted framing, also called a Dutch angle, the frame is not level; it creates an impression of chaos and instability and is often used when a character experiences something unusual or distressing.

title: Pans and tilts: turning the camera in place
description: Camera movement changes framing during a shot; a pan turns the camera horizontally and a tilt swivels it up or down while it stays in one spot.

facts.text: Britannica describes camera movement as moving the camera during shooting to alter framing, scale and shooting angle.
A pan turns the camera horizontally, left or right, sweeping around the scene; the word comes from panorama. A pan can follow someone or reveal something.
A tilt moves the camera from angled down to angled up, or the reverse; tilts are often used to show the scale of a building, starting at its base.

title: Dolly, crane and handheld shots
description: In tracking shots the camera itself travels, often on a dolly; cranes lift it through the air; handheld shooting uses the operator's body; a zoom only enlarges part of the image.

facts.text: In a tracking shot the framing travels through space forward, backward or sideways; the camera often rides a dolly, a small wheeled platform that runs on track or is moved by hand.
A heavy dolly holding the camera and a seated operator can be pushed or driven around the set; if the ground is not smooth, rails like train tracks are laid for it.
In a crane shot the camera, on a crane (a large cantilevered arm), moves through the air above the ground; crane shots can give the viewer a feeling of omniscience over the characters.

When the camera dollies, distances change, so the spatial relationship between objects in the frame changes; a zoom changes only the focal length, enlarging part of the frame without changing perspective, which gives it a flat look.

Handheld shooting uses the camera operator's body as the support; newsreel and wartime operators favored small cameras, later taken up by documentary makers; it is cheap and feels spontaneous but jerky, and gyroscopic Steadicams from the 1970s made smooth moving shots possible.

title: Focal length: wide-angle, normal and telephoto
description: A normal lens (50 mm on 35 mm film) looks like the eye's view; wide-angle lenses take in more and exaggerate depth, telephoto lenses compress it, though perspective really comes from camera distance.

facts.text: A normal lens reproduces perspective similar to the human eye; for 35 mm film a normal lens is 50 mm; shorter lenses are wide-angle and lenses two or more times longer are telephoto.
A wide-angle lens has a short focal length and lets more space into the frame, which makes it handy for shooting in a real room; it exaggerates the distance between foreground and background.
A wide-angle lens exaggerates depth and a telephoto compresses it: a person walking toward the camera seems to approach faster with a wide-angle and slower with a telephoto.

Picture perspective depends on the camera-to-subject distance, not on the lens: from the same distance, different lenses change the area of view but not the perspective, and a telephoto shot is almost always taken from farther away.

title: Depth of field and focus
description: Depth of field is how much of the image, near to far, is sharp; shallow focus isolates one plane to direct attention, and a rack focus shifts focus during a shot.

facts.text: Depth of field is the distance through which elements in an image are in sharp focus; bright light, a narrow aperture and a wide-angle lens tend to give more of it.
Shallow focus keeps only one plane sharp; it directs the viewer's attention to one element without a cut and is very common in close-ups.
Racking focus changes the lens's focus during a shot so one plane goes out of focus as another comes in, steering the viewer's attention and linking two spaces or objects.

title: Three-point lighting
description: The standard lighting of classical narrative film uses a key light, a fill light that softens its shadows, and a backlight that separates the subject from the background.

facts.text: Britannica says lighting helps set the tone and emphasize specific parts of a scene.

Three-point lighting is the standard scheme of classical narrative cinema, and most mainstream films rely on it: a bright key light highlights the subject, a fill light from the opposite side keeps the key's shadows faint, and a backlight picks the subject out from the background.
Documentaries and realist cinema often rely on natural light instead of three-point lighting, to create a sense of authenticity.

title: High-key and low-key lighting
description: High-key lighting raises the fill almost to the key for bright, shadowless images; low-key lighting uses little fill for strong contrast and deep shadows.

facts.text: High-key lighting raises the fill light almost to the level of the key light, producing bright images with few shadows; it is typical of entertainment genres such as musicals and comedies.
Low-key lighting uses very little fill light, creating strong contrast between bright and dark and shadows that obscure parts of the subjects; it is associated with suspense genres such as film noir.

title: The clapperboard marks each take
description: A clapperboard's slate identifies the take, and its snapping arm marks one instant on both picture and sound so editors can synchronize them.

facts.text: A clapper, or clapperboard, is a slate showing information about the take, topped by a hinged arm; its wooden jaws, about a foot long, are snapped together in the picture so the clack registers on both picture and sound.
When sound and picture are recorded separately, the clapper's shared visual and audio cue lets editors match the sound to the images.

title: What a film editor does
description: The editor reviews the footage, chooses the best takes, orders them and trims each shot, turning a pile of takes into the film.

facts.text: A common saying holds that a film is made three times: when the script is written, when it is shot, and again in the editing.
A film editor reviews all the footage, selects the best takes of each shot and orders them, moving from a rough cut to a fine cut.
The terms editing, cutting and montage are often used interchangeably for the process of assembling a film.

title: From splicing film to editing software
description: Editors once cut and spliced celluloid on linear machines like the Moviola; since the 1990s nonlinear digital systems jump straight to any frame.

facts.text: For most of film history, editors physically cut and spliced celluloid on machines that ran footage from the start of a take to its end.
Iwan Serrurier's Moviola, a machine that lets an editor view film while editing, was adapted for film editing in 1924; it was upright, with a single screen.
Since the 1990s editors have used digital nonlinear systems such as Avid, working at a keyboard and jumping instantly to any point in the footage instead of scrolling through every frame.

title: Continuity editing: cuts you do not notice
description: Classical Hollywood's continuity or invisible editing matches direction, position and time from shot to shot so space and time seem unbroken.

facts.text: Continuity editing is a system of cutting that keeps narrative action continuous and clear by matching screen direction, position and time from shot to shot.
The dominant editing style of classical Hollywood, from the 1930s to the 1950s, is sometimes called invisible editing because its cuts are so unobtrusive.
Continuity editing supports the viewer's assumption that space and time run on unbroken from one shot to the next.

title: Match on action
description: Cutting in the middle of a movement and continuing it in the next shot links the shots smoothly, even joining places filmed apart.

facts.text: In a match on action, a movement begun in one shot is picked up where it left off in the next, linking the shots smoothly and reinforcing a sense of consistent space.
In his Biograph films of 1908 to 1913, D. W. Griffith matched action on cuts: a character walks into a doorway outdoors and, in the next shot, enters an interior set, joining places filmed apart.

title: The 180-degree rule
description: Keeping the camera on one side of the axis of action keeps characters on consistent sides of the frame; crossing it needs a reestablishing shot.

facts.text: The 180-degree rule keeps the camera on one side of the axis of action, an imaginary line between the two main elements of a scene, usually two characters.
Following the 180-degree rule keeps each character in a consistent area of the frame, so the left-right geography of the screen stays the same across cuts.
The 180-degree line is not usually crossed unless a reestablishing shot, showing the space again, smooths the change.
Editors can also break continuity on purpose to undermine the viewer's sense of the space.

title: The establishing shot
description: A distant framing that shows how a scene's people, objects and setting are laid out before closer shots begin.

facts.text: An establishing shot, usually a distant framing, shows the spatial relations among the important figures, objects and setting in a scene.

title: Shot, reverse shot
description: Conversations are built from alternating shots of each character, usually close-ups cut to the flow of the dialogue, which lets the editor shape the performances.

facts.text: Shot/reverse shot is two or more shots edited together that alternate between characters, typically in a conversation.
Shot/reverse shot editing uses the eyeline match to connect characters shown separately in close-ups, and its cuts usually follow the flow of the dialogue.
Keeping the camera on a speaker, or cutting to another character's reaction while the line is spoken, gives the same moment a different tone.
Editors trim the ends of shots to make an actor seem to jump in on another's line, or draw out a pause; viewers credit actors with much that comes from editing.

title: The eyeline match
description: A shot of someone looking off-screen followed by what they see; the direction of the look tells you where each person is.

facts.text: In an eyeline match, one shot shows a person looking off-screen in one direction and the next shows what they see; if the person looks left, the next shot implies the looker is off-screen right.

title: Crosscutting builds suspense
description: Alternating two lines of action in different places at once, with shots growing shorter, turns a chase or rescue into suspense.

facts.text: Crosscutting, or parallel editing, alternates shots of two or more lines of action happening in different places, usually at the same time, linking them.
D. W. Griffith became famous for crosscutting in the last-minute rides to the rescue that climax his films.
In The Girl and Her Trust (1912), Griffith cuts between robbers escaping with the heroine on a railroad pump car and the hero chasing them by train.
Intercutting the lines of action creates suspense, and shortening the shots as the chase goes on speeds up the pace; crosscutting became a foundation of film narrative.

title: The jump cut
description: Leaving out part of an action makes time visibly skip, breaking continuity on purpose; Breathless and the French New Wave made it famous.

facts.text: A jump cut leaves out part of an action, producing a visible break between shots and shrinking time in an obvious way.
Jean-Luc Godard's Breathless (1960) used jump cuts that left out parts of the action, and French New Wave films made jump cuts a hallmark of their style.
Jump cuts break with mainstream continuity storytelling and expose a film's artificiality; they can also suggest a character's restless thoughts.

title: The match cut
description: A cut between shots with matching shapes or colors links two things, as when a bone becomes a satellite in 2001: A Space Odyssey.

facts.text: A graphic match, or match cut, joins two shots with strongly similar compositions, such as shape or color, to smooth a transition or suggest a comparison.
In 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), a man-ape tosses a bone into the air and a single cut turns it into an orbiting satellite, a famous match cut from prehistory to the space age.

title: The Kuleshov effect
description: Viewers read an actor's neutral face from the shot placed next to it, because they take the face to be looking at it.

facts.text: Lev Kuleshov (1899 to 1970) was a Soviet film theorist who taught that montage, the cutting and joining of shots, was the most important part of filmmaking.
Kuleshov showed an actor's neutral face followed by different shots, such as soup, a child or a corpse, and viewers read the face as hungry, tender or grieving.
A shot has two values: what it shows by itself, and what it gains when placed next to another shot.
Viewers take the face to be looking at what comes next; a 2024 study describes the sequence as a glance shot of the face followed by an object shot of what is seen.

title: How solid is the Kuleshov experiment?
description: The footage is lost and accounts differ, but a 2016 study found that some sort of Kuleshov effect does exist.

facts.text: The original footage of the experiment is lost, and tellings of it differ, even about which shots were used.
It is doubtful the experiment worked exactly as Kuleshov claimed: the actor's face came from an existing film and likely held an ambiguous expression.
After replications gave conflicting results, a 2016 study with 36 participants found that some sort of Kuleshov effect does exist.

title: Diegetic and non-diegetic sound
description: Diegetic sound comes from the story world and characters could hear it; non-diegetic sound, like most scores, is only for the audience.

facts.text: A film's diegesis is its story world: the objects, events, spaces and characters in it, including things the audience infers but never sees.
Diegetic sound, whether a voice, music or a sound effect, is presented as coming from a source within the film's world.
Non-diegetic sound comes from outside the film's world, as most background music does; only the audience hears it, not the characters.
Internal diegetic sound comes from inside a character's mind, such as their thoughts or sounds they imagine: part of the story world, but heard by no one else in the scene.

title: Foley: sounds made after filming
description: Foley artists perform footsteps and other action sounds in sync with the picture, a craft named after Universal's Jack Foley.

facts.text: A Foley artist creates sounds to accompany specific on-screen actions, such as a person walking, a sword fight or a creaking door.
In the first decades of talkies, microphones were designed mainly to pick up dialogue, so sound effects had to be added at a later step.
The craft is named after Jack Foley, who almost single-handedly developed it in the late 1920s at Universal, adding clapping, laughter and other sounds to Show Boat as the film ran in real time.
Foley artists work on a Foley stage full of props, such as shoes of all kinds, and watch the scene on a large screen so they can create the sounds in sync.
For Titanic, Foley artists made the crackle of frost with frozen lettuce.

title: The sound designer
description: Since Walter Murch's 1979 credit on Apocalypse Now, a sound designer can oversee a film's whole sound concept.

facts.text: In 1979 Francis Ford Coppola gave Walter Murch the credit Sound Designer for Apocalypse Now, the first use of that title in film.
As sound designer, Murch oversaw the film's overall sound concept, including dialogue, sound effects, Foley and the final mix.

title: The sound bridge
description: Letting sound run across a cut, early or late, links two scenes and smooths the transition in continuity editing.

facts.text: A sound bridge carries sound across a cut: the previous scene's sound continues briefly into the next, or the next scene's sound is heard before its image appears.
Sound bridges are one of the most common transitions in continuity editing, stressing the connection between the two scenes.

title: The Jazz Singer brings the talkies
description: Warner Brothers bet on Vitaphone sound-on-disc; The Jazz Singer (1927), with sound for about a quarter of its length, made Hollywood switch to talking pictures.

facts.text: Warner Brothers, then a minor studio, bought Western Electric's Vitaphone sound-on-disc system and debuted it in 1926 with Don Juan.
The Jazz Singer (1927) was the first feature with synchronized dialogue, but only its songs and some conversations, about one-fourth of the film, had recorded sound.
The Jazz Singer's phenomenal success in 1927 virtually ensured Hollywood's conversion to sound and marked the end of the silent-film era.
Al Jolson starred in The Jazz Singer and performed in blackface; the performance has long been studied for what it says about stereotypes.
Blackface minstrelsy, in which white performers caricatured Black people, was built on racial derision and stereotypes.

title: What the switch to sound cost
description: Hollywood converted to sound in under 15 months; microphones and soundproof camera booths made early talkies static until blimps, and some silent stars lost their careers.

facts.text: The American film industry converted to sound in less than 15 months, between late 1927 and 1929, and studios and theaters had to be totally reequipped.
Early sound microphones had a very limited range, so actors had to speak toward them and remain practically motionless while delivering dialogue.
Early sound cameras were enclosed in soundproof glass-paneled booths, called iceboxes because they were hot and stuffy, so the camera could not tilt or dolly.
The immobile camera and actors help explain why many early sound films look static; by 1931 studios used lightweight soundproof camera housings called blimps.

The switch to sound ended some silent careers in Hollywood: the German star Emil Jannings, whose heavy accent suited no English-speaking role, left Hollywood and went back to making films in Germany, including the sound film The Blue Angel (1930).

title: The majors owned the whole chain
description: By 1930 eight studios made nearly all American films; the five majors controlled production, distribution and exhibition, buying theater chains to fill with their own films.

facts.text: By 1930, 95 percent of American film production was concentrated in eight studios.

Five major studios, MGM, Paramount, Warner Brothers, Twentieth Century-Fox and RKO, controlled production, distribution and exhibition; Universal, Columbia and United Artists controlled production and distribution.
Through the 1920s Paramount, MGM and other studios acquired first-run theater chains, and the majors became theater chains that made features, shorts, cartoons and newsreels to fill their own houses.

title: Block booking
description: Under block booking, a theater could license a film it wanted only if it also took other films the distributor released in that period.

facts.text: Block booking was licensing a film or group of films to a theater on condition that it also license other films the distributor released in that period.

title: The star system
description: Early film actors were anonymous; once studios named them, as IMP did with Florence Lawrence in 1910, stars became the most important tool for selling films.

facts.text: Because early film actors were typically kept anonymous, Florence Lawrence became famous as the Biograph Girl.
In 1910 Carl Laemmle hired Lawrence for his new Independent Motion Picture Company, which promoted her by name; she was one of the first movie stars.
The film star was perhaps the most important development in film advertising.

title: Star contracts and studio-made images
description: Studios bound stars with seven-year contracts and morality clauses and manufactured their public images; Olivia de Havilland's lawsuit challenged the contracts.

facts.text: Studios controlled stars' images through morality clauses in contracts and publicists who distributed manufactured star biographies, photos and 'intimate' confessions to fan magazines.
The standard studio-era star contract ran seven years.

Olivia de Havilland won a precedent-setting case against Warner Brothers in the mid-1940s that freed her from a six-month penalty the studio had added to her seven-year contract; she then won Academy Awards for To Each His Own and The Heiress.

title: The Production Code: Hollywood censors itself
description: To head off public outcry and government censorship, the studios adopted the Production Code in 1930 and enforced it from 1934 through an approval office.

facts.text: In 1922 studio heads formed the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America and recruited Will H. Hays to lead it.
Guidelines drafted by Catholic trade publisher Martin Quigley and Jesuit priest Daniel A. Lord were adopted in 1930 as the Motion Picture Production Code.
The Production Code was a set of self-imposed studio guidelines, established in response to public outcry and the threat of government censorship.
In 1934, as the Catholic Legion of Decency called for boycotts of films it found offensive, Hays set up the Production Code Administration under Joseph Breen.
Members of the studios' trade association agreed to distribute only films the Production Code Administration approved.
The code forbade profanity, obscenity and graphic depictions of violence and criminality, and required that good and evil never be confused.

title: Why the Code faded and ratings replaced it
description: Television, foreign films and the 1952 Burstyn v. Wilson ruling weakened the Production Code, and in 1968 an age-based rating system replaced it.

facts.text: After World War II, television and foreign films, both outside the Production Code Administration's jurisdiction, undermined the code.
In Burstyn v. Wilson (1952) the Supreme Court ruled that films communicate ideas and could not face government censorship, weakening the code's hold.
The Production Code regulated films from 1934 to 1968, when it was replaced by the age-based rating system still in use.

title: How three-strip Technicolor made color
description: A beam-splitter sent red, green and blue light to three black-and-white films; dye printing combined them into one color print.

facts.text: Three-strip Technicolor, perfected in 1932, used a beam-splitting cube behind the lens to expose three black-and-white films, one favoring red, one green and one blue.
The three strips were developed and printed separately, the prints passed through matching dyes and laminated together, giving a reasonably faithful approximation of natural color.
Technicolor was introduced in Walt Disney's animated short Flowers and Trees (1932) and the feature film Becky Sharp (1935).

title: Why black and white lasted
description: Costly, rented Technicolor cameras kept color rare; single-strip Eastmancolor replaced them in the 1950s, but most features went color only in the 1960s.

facts.text: Technicolor's three-strip camera was heavy and costly to build.
Technicolor rented its cameras to studios and provided a color consultant, from a team headed by Natalie Kalmus, to each production.
In the early 1950s Technicolor moved to printing from single-strip Eastmancolor negatives, and its three-strip cameras were last used on productions of 1955.
Color was less revolutionary than sound: silent film soon disappeared, but most feature films have been in color only since the 1960s, and black-and-white films are still made.

title: Citizen Kane's deep focus
description: Gregg Toland used fast film, wide-angle lenses at small apertures and arc lamps to keep near and far sharp in Citizen Kane (1941).

facts.text: Citizen Kane (1941), released by RKO, was directed and produced by Orson Welles, who co-wrote it with Herman J. Mankiewicz and starred in it at age 25.
Citizen Kane met considerable critical acclaim but disappointing box-office returns, and its only Oscar was for its screenplay.
Using faster Eastman film stock, wide-angle lenses at small apertures and high-intensity arc lamps, cinematographer Gregg Toland achieved a depth of field approximating the human eye's.
In Citizen Kane, audiences could see sharply detailed characters and objects in all parts of the screen in nearly every scene.

title: Citizen Kane's low angles and flashbacks
description: Citizen Kane shot upward at sets with muslin ceilings that hid microphones, and told Kane's life through flashbacks from five people who knew him.

facts.text: Hollywood sets usually had no ceilings, with lights in the rafters; for Citizen Kane, Toland had muslin ceilings built, which let microphones be placed above them.
In 1941, Citizen Kane's low-angled shots that revealed ceilings appeared powerful and modern.

Citizen Kane opens with Kane's death; a reporter questions people who knew him, and his life unfolds in flashbacks from the shifting, not always reliable accounts of five former intimates, which Welles called prismatic.
Citizen Kane remains one of the most influential films ever made.

title: HUAC, the Hollywood Ten and the blacklist
description: In 1947 HUAC investigated communist influence in films; the Hollywood Ten refused to answer, citing the First Amendment, were imprisoned, and a studio blacklist followed.

facts.text: The House Un-American Activities Committee, established in 1938, began investigating communist influence in Hollywood films in 1947 and called more than 100 witnesses about their own and their associates' alleged communist affiliations.
HUAC held that the American communist movement was foreign-controlled and an immediate threat to national security, and it investigated whether communist propaganda was infiltrating Hollywood films.

The Hollywood Ten, eight screenwriters and two directors, refused to answer HUAC's questions about communist affiliations, invoking the First Amendment to protect their private beliefs and political associations.
The Hollywood Ten were convicted of contempt of Congress and sentenced to six months to one year in prison.
Studio executives fired the Hollywood Ten in the Waldorf Declaration, and an unofficial blacklist refused work to anyone even suspected of communist associations.

title: Writing under false names, and the end of the blacklist
description: Blacklisted writers worked under pseudonyms; Dalton Trumbo's 1960 screen credits helped end the blacklist by the early 1960s.

facts.text: Most of the Hollywood Ten never again worked in Hollywood, but some wrote scripts under pseudonyms; as Robert Rich, Dalton Trumbo won the Academy Award for The Brave One (1956).
In 1960 Trumbo received full screen credit for Exodus and Spartacus, and the blacklist disappeared by the early 1960s.
HUAC was criticized for violating First Amendment rights; its influence waned by the 1960s, and it was dissolved in 1975.

title: The 1948 Paramount ruling
description: In United States v. Paramount Pictures (1948) the Supreme Court upheld findings against block booking and price fixing, and the decrees forced the majors to sell their theaters.

facts.text: United States v. Paramount Pictures was an antitrust case decided by the Supreme Court on May 3, 1948, in an opinion by Justice William O. Douglas.
The Court upheld findings that block booking was illegal and that the defendants had illegally fixed minimum admission prices that exhibitors agreed to charge.

In the 92 US cities with populations over 100,000, at least 70 percent of first-run theaters were affiliated with one or more of the five majors, which owned or controlled theaters through subsidiaries or affiliates.
In 1948 the antitrust case ended in the Paramount decrees, which forced the studios to divest their theater chains and mandated competition in exhibition.

title: After Paramount: the studio system weakened
description: Separating production from exhibition made filmmaking less stable and severely weakened the studio system.

facts.text: By cutting the link between production and exhibition, the Paramount consent decrees made film production a much less stable undertaking.
The 1948 Paramount decrees severely weakened the Hollywood studio system.

title: Television takes the audience
description: Movie attendance peaked in 1946; network television offered moving pictures at home, attendance fell by almost half by 1956, and Hollywood turned to color and widescreen.

facts.text: In 1946, when two-thirds of Americans went to the movies at least once a week, the studios earned record-breaking profits.
Network television broadcasting in the 1940s gave Hollywood its first real competition for Americans' leisure time by offering movies in the home.
By 1956 US movie attendance was down almost 50 percent from its 1946 peak.
Hollywood used color and widescreen to differentiate its films from television.

title: Cinerama and CinemaScope
description: Cinerama (1952) used three projectors and proved too costly; CinemaScope (1953) squeezed a wide image onto standard 35 mm film with special lenses and spread across the industry.

facts.text: Cinerama, first presented in New York City in 1952 with This Is Cinerama, used three synchronized projectors, each projecting one-third of the picture on a wide, curving screen.
Cinerama was a popular novelty, but its costs were prohibitive, and it was abandoned in the 1960s.
CinemaScope used a special camera lens to squeeze a wide picture onto standard 35 mm film; a projection lens restored it on a screen two and a half times as wide as it was high.
Twentieth Century-Fox introduced CinemaScope in The Robe (1953), and by the late 1950s most films released by the major studios were made for wide-screen projection.

title: The studio era: one company, every step
description: In the studio era a major studio controlled every stage of a feature, from contract stars and code approval to distribution and its own theaters.

facts.text: Between 1930 and 1945, the studio system produced features whose every stage, from conception through exhibition, was carefully controlled.

title: A genre promises the familiar and the new
description: A genre promises audiences something like what they enjoyed before, yet also something new; long familiarity trains viewers to expect its characters, music, lighting and plot devices.

facts.text: Britannica says genres promise audiences something similar to what they have enjoyed in the past, yet also something quite new and different.
Viewers largely knew what to expect from a genre film: they recognized its stars or characters and were sensitive to its music, lighting and plot devices from long familiarity.
Most genres are defined by subject matter or setting, such as the western, the gangster film, the police thriller and the science-fiction film.

title: Why studios loved genres
description: A studio making several films in one genre could reuse sets and costumes and keep the same personnel on it, building a routine that made filmmaking quicker and often better.

facts.text: A studio making half a dozen police thrillers in one year could save time and money by reusing sets, costumes and other items.
Studios could assign the same writers, directors, crews and actors to a genre, building a routine that often made filmmaking quicker and better.

title: The Western: America's own genre
description: Set in the American West of roughly the 1850s to 1900, the Western is basically an American creation; its pattern dates from 1903, Stagecoach revived it in 1939, and it later filled TV screens.

facts.text: The western is set in the American West, usually from the 1850s to the end of the 19th century.
Britannica calls the western basically an American creation, and the Library of Congress calls it a historically inspired genre invented in the United States.
Britannica dates the western film from The Great Train Robbery (1903), which set the pattern for many films that followed.
Cowboys, the town sheriff and the U.S. marshal are staple figures of the western, whose conflicts are often settled by violence and physical courage.
By 1939 the western had long been relegated to B-movie status; John Ford's Stagecoach, starring John Wayne, revitalized the genre with its critical and commercial success.
TV westerns such as Gunsmoke and Bonanza drew large audiences in the late 1950s and the 1960s.

title: How Westerns pictured Native Americans
description: Conflict between pioneers and Native Americans is a basic Western theme; early films showed Native Americans with little understanding, and later Westerns shifted sympathy toward them.

facts.text: Conflict between white pioneers and Native Americans is one of the western's basic themes, and earlier films showed Native Americans with remarkably little understanding or appreciation.
Later westerns shifted sympathy toward Native Americans, among them John Ford's Cheyenne Autumn (1964), Little Big Man (1970) and Dances with Wolves (1990).

title: Musicals sing what speech can't carry
description: A musical film integrates musical numbers into its plot; over the 1930s and 1940s plot and music grew more unified, until song and dance carried a film's key emotional moments.

facts.text: Britannica defines a musical film as a motion picture whose plot integrates musical numbers.
Fred Astaire's dances with Ginger Rogers at RKO, as in Top Hat (1935), worked as sophisticated statements of romantic love.
Late-1930s and 1940s musicals such as The Wizard of Oz (1939) showed a trend toward greater unification of plot and music.
In Singin' in the Rain (1952), song and dance rather than dialogue carry the important moments; Gene Kelly swings from a lamppost celebrating new love.

title: Berkeley's spectacle and Astaire's simplicity
description: Busby Berkeley filmed dancers from overhead in geometric patterns inside well-worn stories; by the mid-1930s dance teams led by Astaire, filmed in full figure with few cuts, took over.

facts.text: Busby Berkeley placed the camera directly above his performers to show them moving in precise geometric formations.
In the early 1930s Berkeley presented elaborately staged dance sequences within well-worn stories, in films such as 42nd Street (1933).
By the mid-1930s, singing and dancing teams such as Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers had overtaken Berkeley's spectacles in popularity.
Fred Astaire simplified the movie musical: dancers were shot in full figure, with a minimum of edits and camera angles.

title: Screwball comedy's sparring couples
description: Screwball comedies of the 1930s and 1940s paired seemingly mismatched lovers in zany situations and rapid, overlapping dialogue; It Happened One Night helped set the pattern.

facts.text: It Happened One Night (1934), Frank Capra's comedy about a runaway heiress and a reporter, was the first film to win all five major Academy Awards and helped establish screwball conventions.
Screwball conventions include seemingly mismatched lovers in unlikely romances, off-the-wall characters and zany situations.
Screwball comedies often showed elegantly dressed couples in opulent Art Deco settings whose shared mischief proved them suited as lovers.
In Bringing Up Baby (1938), Katharine Hepburn's eccentric heiress pursues Cary Grant's bookish paleontologist through a series of farcical mishaps.
Howard Hawks made overlapping dialogue a trademark, and His Girl Friday (1940) is known for its rapid-fire delivery.
For His Girl Friday, Hawks changed The Front Page's newspaper editor and reporter from two men to a man (Cary Grant) and a woman (Rosalind Russell).

title: Why screwball couples spar
description: Depression-era studios wanted stories of people beating adversity, and the Hays Code banned explicit sexual references, so verbal sparring and physical comedy stood in for sex.

facts.text: During the Depression, with film attendance in decline, studios sought audiences with stories that showed protagonists triumphing over adversity.
The Hays Code, Hollywood's own guidelines from 1934 to 1968, banned explicit mention of sexual relationships, so verbal sparring and physical comedy took the place of sexuality.

title: Why people choose to be scared
description: Horror aims to cause fear or dread; a 2020 haunted-house study found enjoyment peaks at a just-right amount of fear, which researchers liken to play.

facts.text: Britannica defines a horror film as one calculated to cause intense repugnance, fear or dread.
In a 2020 study, researchers fitted 110 visitors to a commercial haunted house in Vejle, Denmark, with heart rate monitors.
Recreational fear is the mixed experience of feeling fear and enjoyment at the same time.
Enjoyment followed an inverted U: visitors who were barely scared or too scared enjoyed the haunted house less than those at a just-right level of fear.
The researchers compare recreational fear to play: enjoyment comes from just-right departures from a person's normal physiological state.

title: Horror by suggestion: Cat People
description: Val Lewton's Cat People (1942) never shows its monster; shadows, low light and long silences let the viewer's imagination build the dread.

facts.text: Cat People (1942), produced by Val Lewton for RKO, never shows its heroine Irena in cat form and relies on suggestion and the viewer's imagination.
Britannica notes Cat People for its masterful use of shadows and low lighting to create suspense.
Lewton worked on skeletal budgets, and his films often hold silence for long periods to build dread.

title: Film noir's dark look
description: French critics named American crime films of the 1940s film noir; their signature is stark high-contrast lighting that isolates the hero, with roots in German Expressionism.

facts.text: French critics coined the term film noir, meaning dark film, after World War II, admiring American crime films for their cynical characters and dark, brooding style.
Banned in occupied countries during the war, these American films became available throughout Europe beginning in 1946.
Stark high-contrast lighting, film noir's most notable visual feature, underscores the isolation of the typical noir hero.
Film noir's shadowy style traces back to German Expressionist films such as The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920).
Typical noir images include rain-soaked streets and flashing neon signs.

title: Why film noir flourished in the 1940s
description: Noir drew stories from hard-boiled crime novels, reflected postwar disillusionment, and attracted European-born directors who felt like outsiders in Hollywood.

facts.text: The Maltese Falcon (1941), John Huston's first film as director, adapted Dashiell Hammett's 1930 hard-boiled detective novel and is considered by some the first major work of noir.
Double Indemnity (1944), directed by Billy Wilder, adapted a novel by James M. Cain, with Raymond Chandler as co-writer.
Britannica links film noir to postwar disillusionment: an unstable peacetime economy, McCarthyism and the looming threat of atomic warfare.
European-born directors such as Billy Wilder and Fritz Lang, trained to stress style, often felt like outsiders in the Hollywood studio system and were drawn to noir.

title: 1950s science fiction and the atom
description: 1950s science fiction turned atomic-age fear into story: a visitor warns Earth about its bombs, and bomb tests breed giant ants.

facts.text: In The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951), directed by Robert Wise, the visitor Klaatu lands in Washington, D.C., and warns that humanity's atomic weapons threaten other civilizations.
Britannica calls The Day the Earth Stood Still a classic that reflects the fears of the Cold War and the early atomic age.
In Them! (1954), directed by Gordon Douglas, giant ants mutated by atomic bomb tests in the New Mexico desert threaten humanity.
Britannica calls Them! arguably the best of the 1950s giant atomic-mutant creature movies.

title: Invasion stories as mirrors of their time
description: Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956) shows pod people replacing humans; made at the height of the Cold War, it has been read as an allegory of many fears, though its director denied any political intent.

facts.text: In Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956), directed by Don Siegel, aliens grow in seedpods and take over people's bodies while they sleep, leaving duplicates without human emotion.
Made at the height of the Cold War, the film has been read as an allegory of Cold War paranoia, fear of McCarthyism, alienation in mass society or loss of autonomy under communism.
Siegel dismissed such readings and said he did not intend a political message.

title: Hitchcock's bomb: surprise versus suspense
description: Hitchcock contrasted a bomb that explodes without warning (15 seconds of surprise) with one the audience knows about (15 minutes of suspense), because the informed audience participates.

facts.text: In 1962 François Truffaut interviewed Alfred Hitchcock at length; the resulting book, Le Cinéma selon Alfred Hitchcock, was published in 1966.
