In Hitchcock's example, a bomb under a table explodes without warning during an ordinary chat, giving the audience 15 seconds of surprise.
If the audience sees the bomb planted, knows it will explode at one o'clock and sees a clock at a quarter to one, the same scene gives 15 minutes of suspense.
Hitchcock said the harmless conversation becomes fascinating because the audience is participating in the scene.

title: Suspense by telling: Double Indemnity
description: A film can build a whole story on what the audience already knows: Double Indemnity reveals who committed the crime at the start, trading a mystery for suspense.

facts.text: Double Indemnity lets the audience know who committed the crime from the start, making it a character-driven drama rather than a mystery.

title: Parody: a genre's rules played for laughs
description: Parodies such as Blazing Saddles and Young Frankenstein (both 1974) imitate a genre's conventions and look closely enough for audiences to recognize them, then play them for laughs.

facts.text: Blazing Saddles (1974), directed by Mel Brooks, spoofs westerns with a Black sheriff at its center, satirizing racial prejudice and western conventions.
Young Frankenstein (1974), also by Mel Brooks, parodies Universal's Frankenstein films; its black-and-white cinematography replicated the look of Bride of Frankenstein (1935).

title: Revisionist films turn a genre's rules around
description: Acclaimed films often invoke a genre's conventions only to break them; revisionist Westerns such as Unforgiven (1992) turned the genre's codes against themselves.

facts.text: Britannica notes that often the most acclaimed films invoke a genre's conventions only to break them down.
Britannica traces the western from Stagecoach to Unforgiven (1992), which it describes as an ironic perversion of the genre's codes.
Unforgiven, a revisionist western, took an unsentimental look at frontier violence and won Academy Awards for best picture and best director.

title: Where one genre ends: setting, subject or style
description: Most genres are defined by subject or setting, but the musical can be about almost anything, and film noir is often called a style that crosses genres rather than a genre.

facts.text: Britannica defines film noir as a style of filmmaking and notes controversy over whether it is a genre or subgenre or only stylistic elements common to many genres.
The noir label applies mostly to crime dramas, but some critics cite certain westerns and comedies as film noir.
The musical often has a show-business setting, but it is not so narrowly restricted and can be about almost any subject.

title: Neorealism: cinema out of the rubble
description: After Fascism fell, Italian filmmakers shot on real, war-damaged streets with ordinary-looking casts, as in Rossellini's Open City.

facts.text: Italian Neorealism, rooted in the 1920s but held back for nearly two decades by Fascist control, emerged in great strength after the Fascist regime fell at the end of World War II.
Neorealist films had a documentary-like objectivity; their actors either were or looked like ordinary people involved in commonplace situations.
Roberto Rossellini's Open City (1945) was shot just months after the Allies liberated Rome, using the city's rubble-strewn streets and a cast many of whom were not actors.
The BFI reports that Open City was made on the streets of war-ravaged Rome with scraps of 35mm film stock.

title: Bicycle Thieves: real streets, real faces
description: De Sica's Bicycle Thieves (1948) told a small story of a poor man's stolen bicycle, shot on location with non-professional actors.

facts.text: Vittorio De Sica's Bicycle Thieves (1948), written by Cesare Zavattini, follows a poor man in postwar Rome whose bicycle, essential for his job, is stolen; he and his son search for it.
In Bicycle Thieves, Antonio's new job pasting posters on walls requires a bicycle.
Bicycle Thieves was shot on location with non-professional actors, Lamberto Maggiorani and Enzo Staiola, as the father and son.
De Sica was drawn to Lamberto Maggiorani's callused worker's hands and the way he moved, both of which signified his class.

title: The New Wave: critics become directors
description: Critics from Cahiers du cinéma, such as Truffaut and Godard, reacted against polished French films and began directing their own in the late 1950s.

facts.text: The New Wave was the style of highly individualistic French directors of the late 1950s, among them Claude Chabrol, François Truffaut, Alain Resnais and Jean-Luc Godard.
Many New Wave directors, including Truffaut and Godard, were associated with the film magazine Cahiers du cinéma, where they had written as critics in the 1950s.
For eight years at Cahiers du cinéma, Truffaut was the most truculent critic of contemporary French cinema, which he considered stale and conventional.
The New Wave was a reaction against the commercial production system: the well-constructed plot, the merely craftsmanlike approach and the French 'tradition of quality'.
Truffaut's semiautobiographical The 400 Blows (1959) won the best direction prize at the 1959 Cannes festival, establishing him as a leader of the New Wave.

title: Breathless: cheap tools become a style
description: Godard's Breathless was shot handheld on a low budget and cut with visible jump cuts that break continuity.

facts.text: Breathless (1960) used low-budget guerrilla techniques: cinematographer Raoul Coutard shot handheld and was once pushed in a wheelchair because the production could not afford tracks.
To shorten Breathless, Godard cut within scenes rather than removing whole ones, producing jump cuts that break continuity and draw attention to the filmmaking.
The New Wave helped demonstrate that films could achieve both commercial and artistic success.

title: Rashomon: one event, four versions
description: Kurosawa's Rashomon shows a single crime recalled differently by four people, a meditation on the nature of truth.

facts.text: Kurosawa Akira's Rashomon (1950), adapted from two Akutagawa stories, shows a rape and a murder recollected in distinctly different ways by four people: a samurai, his wife, a bandit and a woodcutter.

Showing the same event as seen by different people caught audiences' imagination and advanced the idea of cinema as a way to probe a deep philosophical problem; Britannica calls Rashomon a meditation on the nature of truth.

title: Rashomon's prize opens the West
description: Rashomon's Golden Lion at Venice in 1951 brought Japanese film serious attention worldwide.

facts.text: Rashomon won the Golden Lion, the top prize at the 1951 Venice Film Festival, the first time a Japanese film had won such high international acclaim.
After Rashomon's success, Japanese films attracted serious attention all over the world, and new export markets opened in the West.

title: Ozu's low, still camera
description: Ozu framed scenes low, as if seated on a tatami mat, barely moved the camera, avoided fades and dissolves, and used pillow shots between scenes.

facts.text: Ozu framed scenes from a low angle, as if seated on a tatami mat, used a 50mm lens exclusively and kept camera movement to a minimum.
Ozu almost totally abandoned devices such as camera movement in favour of straight pictorial shots.
In Tokyo Story, fades and dissolves are conspicuous by their absence, and tracking shots are rare.
Critic Noël Burch named Ozu's short, place-setting shots between scenes, of seas, mountains, boats, train tracks, buildings and rooms, 'pillow shots'; they keep his measured rhythm.

title: Ozu and the drama of ordinary families
description: Ozu's shomin-geki found drama in lower-middle-class family life, as in Tokyo Story's visit of an aged couple to their children.

facts.text: Ozu was a leading director of the shomin-geki, 'common-people's drama', a genre about lower-middle-class Japanese family life that grew up at the Shochiku studio.
Tokyo Story (1953) follows an aged couple on their first trip to Tokyo, from their seaside hometown of Onomichi, to visit the families of their two eldest children.

title: Ray learns from neorealism
description: Satyajit Ray, an advertising art director and book designer, was inspired by Bicycle Thieves to film on location with non-professionals.

facts.text: Before filmmaking, Satyajit Ray worked as an art director at a British advertising agency and became a leading Indian typographer and book-jacket designer.
Ray illustrated an edition of Bibhutibhushan Banerjee's novel Pather Panchali, whose possibilities as a film began to intrigue him.
Ray was inspired by De Sica's The Bicycle Thief, which showed a film could be made on location with non-professional actors; meeting Jean Renoir in Bengal in 1949 also encouraged him.

title: Pather Panchali brings realism to Indian film
description: Ray's Pather Panchali (1955), made against the odds, gave a naturalistic portrait of a poor Bengal village family and won at Cannes.

facts.text: Bengali producers distrusted Ray's unconventional approach, so he began shooting in late 1952 with his own money and an inexperienced crew; with reluctant help from the West Bengal government, the film took two and a half years.

Pather Panchali follows a boy, Apu, growing up in an impoverished rural community in Bengal; in one of its most memorable scenes, Apu and his sister run through a paddy field to glimpse a passing train.
The BFI describes Pather Panchali as a naturalistic portrait of ordinary lives in a rural family, with all its mischief, discoveries, joys and tragedies.
Pather Panchali (1955) was a commercial and critical success and won a major award at the 1956 Cannes festival, which let Ray make the rest of the Apu trilogy.

title: Why Hindi films sing
description: Song and dance, inherited from Parsi theatre and present since the first talkie in 1931, run through every genre of popular Hindi film and drive box office.

facts.text: Sound arrived in Indian cinema in 1931 with the first talkie, the Hindi-language Alam Ara.
Alam Ara was advertised as 'All talking, all singing, all dancing' and contained seven song sequences.
Parsi theatre, which flourished between the 1850s and 1930s, was a forerunner to Bollywood, combining folk and musical theatre traditions.
Bollywood, a blend of 'Bombay' and 'Hollywood', names the Hindi-language film industry.
Unlike Hollywood, where the musical is one genre, Bollywood puts song and dance into any and all of its other genres.
In Bollywood, film soundtracks and choreographed set pieces are often the engines that drive box-office results.

title: Playback singing
description: Playback singers prerecord film songs and the stars lip-sync to them on screen.

facts.text: Playback singers prerecord a film's songs, and the stars lip-sync to them on screen; the singers themselves do not appear.
Lata Mangeshkar, an iconic Indian playback singer, recorded songs for the soundtracks of more than 2,000 Indian films.

title: Bruce Lee and realistic kung fu
description: Bruce Lee's realistic, fast martial arts made Hong Kong action famous, and Enter the Dragon joined Hong Kong and U.S. producers.

facts.text: Bruce Lee's first Hong Kong films, The Big Boss (1971) and Fist of Fury (1972), were huge successes; audiences embraced The Big Boss's realistic martial arts.
The speed of Lee's punches and the fluidity of his kicks, rooted in rigorous training, gave his films a fresh sense of authenticity and realism.
Enter the Dragon (1973), the first joint venture between Hong Kong- and U.S.-based production companies, was a worldwide hit; Lee died on July 20, 1973, before its release.

title: Opera training, stunts and wirework
description: Peking opera training shaped Jackie Chan and Yuen Woo-ping, whose comedy, real stunts and wirework reshaped action filmmaking worldwide.

facts.text: From age 7 to 17, Jackie Chan studied acrobatics, singing, martial arts and mime at a strict boarding school that trained students for Peking opera.
Yuen Woo-ping was born into a family of Peking Opera performers, a tradition in which drama, martial arts, acrobatics and dance were inseparable.
In 1978 Jackie Chan found his signature bumbling physical comedy in Snake in the Eagle's Shadow and Drunken Master, Yuen Woo-ping's first two films as director.
Jackie Chan is known for performing his own dangerous stunts; a fall while filming Armour of God (1986) fractured his skull.
Yuen Woo-ping's work on The Matrix (1999), combining Hong Kong wirework (harnesses and cables that propel and suspend performers) with science fiction, changed how Hollywood approaches action.

title: Why Nigerian film turned to video
description: The naira's fall in the 1980s made film equipment scarce and theaters hard to reach, and celluloid production stopped.

facts.text: In the 1980s the devaluation of the Nigerian naira made film equipment hard to come by and movie theaters increasingly inaccessible; by the early 1990s celluloid film production had ceased.

title: Nollywood: an industry on videotape
description: Living in Bondage (1992) went straight to VHS, launching a fast, low-budget video industry later nicknamed Nollywood.

facts.text: Britannica dates Nigeria's video film industry to 1992 and Living in Bondage, which was distributed straight to VHS, became a smash hit and revolutionized Nigerian cinema.
Nollywood films were largely low-budget, and most were shot in about a week.
Nollywood includes films in Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa and other languages of Nigeria.
The word 'Nollywood', from Nigeria and Hollywood, first appeared in a New York Times headline in 2002.

title: Venice and Cannes
description: Venice (1932) is the oldest film festival; Cannes, planned for 1939, opened in 1946. Their prizes make films known abroad.

facts.text: The Venice Film Festival, founded in 1932 and officially part of the Venice Biennale, is the world's oldest film festival; its top prize is the Golden Lion.
Cannes began as Philippe Erlanger's idea for an event to replace Venice's festival and offer the world a festival free of pressure and constraints.
The first Cannes festival was to open on 1 September 1939, the day Germany invaded Poland; it finally took place in 1946.
Cannes awarded its first Palme d'Or in 1955, to Delbert Mann's Marty.
The main auditorium of Cannes's Palais des Festivals bears the name of cinema pioneer Louis Lumière and hosts the Festival de Cannes ceremonies.

title: Festivals as marketplaces
description: At Cannes, producers and distributors view films and sign contracts; its Marché du Film became official in 1959.

facts.text: Cannes became an international marketplace where producers and distributors could exchange ideas, view films and sign contracts.
The Marché du Film, the Cannes film market held unofficially since 1946, was given official status in 1959.

title: Go-betweens carry films across borders
description: People and festivals carried films abroad: Stramigioli sent Rashomon to Venice, and Open City won at the first Cannes.

facts.text: Italifilm president Giuliana Stramigioli recommended Rashomon to the selection committee in Venice, where it won the Golden Lion in 1951.
Open City was one of the films awarded the Grand Prix, the festival's top prize, at the first Cannes festival in 1946, when the prize was shared among films from many countries.

title: Television grew out of radio's networks
description: American TV borrowed radio's networks: NBC's 1926 radio chain, its Blue network that became ABC, and NBC's own TV network by 1948.

facts.text: Television was first regarded by many as 'radio with pictures.'
In 1948 television was still in its experimental stage, and radio remained the number one broadcast medium.
NBC was formed in 1926; on November 15, 1926, 25 radio stations in 21 cities carried its first network program from New York.
After the FCC refused licenses to companies running more than one network, NBC was forced to sell its Blue radio network, which became ABC.
NBC began operating its first television station in 1939, and by 1948 its TV network had 47 stations.

title: Radio's stars and sponsors came to TV
description: Radio stars hesitated, then followed Milton Berle into TV; CBS lured NBC's radio stars in 1948; and advertising, radio's way of paying, became TV's too.

facts.text: Most of radio's biggest stars, such as Jack Benny, Bob Hope, and George Burns and Gracie Allen, were at first reluctant to risk their careers on television.

Milton Berle, who had had little success on radio, starred in NBC's Texaco Star Theatre from 1948; it was TV's first hit and led to a dramatic increase in TV set sales, earning him the name Mr. Television.
When Texaco Star Theatre debuted in 1948, fewer than 2 percent of US homes had a TV set; by 1956, TV was in 70 percent of homes.
In 1948 CBS chief William S. Paley signed radio stars away from NBC, including Jack Benny, George Burns and Gracie Allen, and Amos 'n' Andy's creators; they proved as popular on TV as on radio.
CBS began as a radio network in the late 1920s and grew under William S. Paley.
Advertising became the principal means of support for broadcasting in the United States; sponsored network programs furnished revenue to both the network and its stations.
On NBC radio, breakout hits on the Blue network were often moved to the more popular Red network at the request of sponsors.

title: Three networks ruled prime time
description: Four networks started regular schedules in 1948; DuMont folded, and ABC, CBS and NBC held more than 90 percent of the prime-time audience in the late 1970s.

facts.text: Regular programming on the four networks, ABC, CBS, NBC and DuMont, was scarce until the fall of 1948; DuMont folded in the mid-1950s.
Prime time is the evening block from 8 to 11 PM Eastern time.
In the late 1970s, more than 90 percent of the US prime-time viewing audience watched ABC, CBS or NBC.

title: The network era's shared screen
description: With nearly every home tuned to the same three networks, TV became cultural glue: a big event like the 1960 debate reached most of the country at once.

facts.text: By 1960 nearly 90 percent of American homes had a television.
On September 26, 1960, the first televised presidential debate, between John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon, was simulcast on all three networks and reached a then-record audience of about 70 million.
Britannica calls radio and television a kind of cultural glue: from 1929 to 1989, nearly the entire country, young and old, rich and poor, fed from the same cultural trough.
Control of television by three companies produced a unified mass culture whose products were experienced by nearly everyone.

title: Live TV drama and the anthology series
description: Early network TV was mostly live; anthology series staged a new play each week, and writers such as Paddy Chayefsky and Rod Serling made their names.

facts.text: In the early 1950s most network television was broadcast live; by the early 1960s most was recorded.
Most TV plays of the era were anthology dramas, weekly series presenting original and adapted plays under one title, such as Kraft Television Theatre (1947 to 1958) and Studio One (1948 to 1958).
Young writers such as Paddy Chayefsky, Rod Serling and Gore Vidal wrote highly regarded teleplays for the network anthology series.
Marty began as a 1953 television play and became a 1955 film that won the Academy Award for best picture.

title: From kinescope to videotape
description: Before 1956, TV could be recorded only by filming a monitor (a kinescope), which was costly and poor; Ampex's videotape, and filmed Hollywood series, ended the live era.

facts.text: Before videotape, the only way to record TV was on film: a movie camera pointed at a TV monitor made a kinescope, which was developed and later projected for broadcast in other time zones.
Kinescope recordings were poor in quality and expensive, since the film could be used only once; by 1954 TV broadcasters were using more raw film than the entire movie industry.
In 1956 Ampex introduced the first practical videotape recorder for TV stations and networks, replacing kinescope film.
On November 30, 1956, CBS taped a live New York newscast on an Ampex recorder in Hollywood and rebroadcast it hours later to the West Coast.
TV production moved to the Los Angeles area, the live theatrical style gave way to shows recorded on film, and filmed shows could earn income indefinitely from reruns.

title: What a sitcom is
description: A situation comedy is a half-hour series with a continuing cast in the same setting, week after week; I Love Lucy grew from a radio comedy.

facts.text: The sitcom was a 30-minute format featuring a continuing cast of characters that appeared in the same setting week after week.
I Love Lucy (CBS, 1951 to 1957), starring Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz, debuted in October 1951; it was shot on film in Hollywood rather than broadcast live from New York.
I Love Lucy was adapted for TV from My Favorite Husband, a CBS radio comedy in which Lucille Ball starred from 1948.
I Love Lucy's early episodes took place mostly in a New York apartment building, where Lucy and Ricky Ricardo lived near their landlords and friends, Fred and Ethel Mertz.

title: I Love Lucy's three-camera method
description: Filmed on 35 mm with three cameras before a live audience and edited on a four-headed Moviola, I Love Lucy set the sitcom standard and could be rerun.

facts.text: Most TV shows were then made in the East, broadcast live there and shown to western time zones as kinescope copies, which a Library of Congress specialist likened to watching TV through a cheesecloth; Ball and Arnaz chose to produce their show in Hollywood.

Cinematographer Karl Freund and director Marc Daniels are generally credited with filming I Love Lucy with three cameras in front of a live audience, the technique that became the standard for sitcoms.
I Love Lucy was shot on 35 mm film before a live audience, with one lighting system for the whole set.

With three motion picture cameras, I Love Lucy could be filmed continuously and in sequence, like a stage play; editor Dann Cahn cut it on a Moviola with four heads, three for picture and one for sound.
Because it was produced on film, I Love Lucy could be shown again, and in 1955 it became one of the first series broadcast as reruns.

title: The evening news grows to half an hour
description: Network evening newscasts ran 15 minutes until 1963, when CBS under Walter Cronkite, and then the others, expanded to half an hour.

facts.text: In 1963 the network evening news programs expanded from 15 minutes to half an hour.
Walter Cronkite became anchor of the CBS evening news in 1962; soon after, its 15 minutes became 30, the first half-hour nightly news show on American network television.

title: Vietnam, the first television war
description: Vietnam was the first televised war: evening news showed film, flown in by air, of planes and patrols, and in 1968 Cronkite went to see for himself.

facts.text: The Vietnam War was the first war to be televised; Americans regularly saw film of airplanes flying, often dropping bombs, and troops on patrol, sometimes in combat.
Film of the Vietnam War usually reached the networks as cans of film shipped by air, arriving a few days later.
In 1968 Walter Cronkite left the anchor desk to report from Vietnam after the Tet Offensive and declared that the war could end only in a stalemate.

title: From single sponsors to commercials
description: After the rigged quiz shows of the late 1950s, networks took shows away from single sponsors and sold short commercial slots, like ad pages in a magazine.

facts.text: In 1958 former contestants revealed that big-money TV quiz shows were rigged and contestants coached; a House subcommittee held hearings in 1959.
After the quiz show scandals, networks grew wary of single-sponsor programs and sold advertising time in 15-, 30- and 60-second units, taking control from sponsors and ad agencies.

Producers took full control of shows and stations sold commercial time, following the model of magazines and newspapers; removing advertisers from the shows removed their urge to interfere with content.

title: Nielsen ratings price the audience
description: From 1950 Nielsen measured viewing in a sample of homes with Audimeters and diaries; ratings and shares set what advertising on each program costs.

facts.text: From 1950 A.C. Nielsen rated TV shows using a sample of more than 1,000 TV homes; each had a small box, the Audimeter, attached to the set to record when it was on and what channel it was tuned to, and a smaller group kept viewing diaries.
A Nielsen rating of 20 means 20 percent of all US TV households tuned in to a program; a 30 share means 30 percent of the people watching TV at that time watched it.
Commercial networks use ratings, in part, to set advertising rates for each program and to decide which programs to continue or cancel.

title: The Public Broadcasting Act of 1967
description: Calls for less commercial TV led to the 1967 Act, proposed by the Carnegie Commission, which created the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and led to PBS and NPR.

facts.text: After the quiz show hearings, columnists such as Walter Lippmann called for a new kind of television modeled on the BBC, calls that led toward a publicly funded system.
On November 7, 1967, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Public Broadcasting Act, which created the Corporation for Public Broadcasting.
The Public Broadcasting Act was proposed by the Carnegie Commission on educational television.
Johnson said the Corporation for Public Broadcasting would get part of its support from the government but be carefully guarded from government or party control.
The Public Broadcasting Act led to the establishment of the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, PBS and NPR.

title: Sesame Street teaches with TV's own tricks
description: The Children's Television Workshop built Sesame Street (1969) with educators and researchers to prepare low-income children for school, borrowing commercial TV's pace and repetition.

facts.text: The first episode of Sesame Street, sponsored by the letters W, S and E and the numbers 2 and 3, aired in the fall of 1969.
Joan Ganz Cooney, a New York public TV producer, founded the Children's Television Workshop in 1968 with backing from the Carnegie and Ford Foundations and the US Commissioner of Education.
Sesame Street was designed by education professionals and child psychologists to help low-income and minority children aged 2 to 5 arrive at school better prepared.
Cooney consulted dozens of educators and set up a collaboration with educators and child development researchers to plan the show.
Sesame Street debuted in 1969 on National Educational Television, which became PBS in 1970, and features animations, live actors and Jim Henson's Muppets.
Cooney based Sesame Street's fast pace, repeated segments and mix of formats on 1960s commercial television.
Signing the Public Broadcasting Act, Johnson said the new corporation would try to prove that what educates can also be exciting.

title: Cable's start, HBO and CNN
description: Cable began in the late 1940s to fix poor reception; HBO (1972) sold commercial-free films and went national by satellite in 1975; CNN (1980) brought 24-hour news.

facts.text: US cable-television systems began in the late 1940s to improve reception of network broadcasts in remote and hilly areas.
Some cable systems can deliver 50 or more channels.
HBO started in 1972 showing uncut, commercial-free movies, and cable subscribers paid extra for it.
In 1975 HBO became the first American network to deliver its programming by satellite, and thus the first national cable channel.
CNN began in 1980 and ushered in the era of 24-hour television news.

title: Cable splits the audience
description: As cable reached most homes, the three networks' share fell, and channels aimed at special interests divided viewers, ending the shared network era.

facts.text: Only 8 percent of US households had basic cable in 1970, 23 percent in 1980, and nearly 60 percent by the end of the 1980s.
By 1989 the three networks' share of the prime-time audience was down to 67 percent.
In the 1990s the number of cable services aimed at specific audiences with specialized interests grew faster than ever before, dividing the audience into smaller and smaller segments.
Britannica says the era of a unified mass culture shaped by three networks ended, in effect, in the 1990s, when audiences stopped watching the same things at the same time.

title: Streaming puts viewers in charge
description: Netflix went from DVDs by mail (1997) to streaming (2007) to whole seasons at once (2013), letting viewers watch at their own pace on any screen.

facts.text: Netflix was founded in 1997 by Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph as a DVD-rental service; subscribers ordered online and received discs by mail.
In 2007 Netflix introduced streaming, letting subscribers watch directly over the Internet.
In February 2013 Netflix made all 13 first-season episodes of House of Cards available at once, instead of one episode a week.
Viewers quickly embraced having all episodes of a new season to watch at their own pace, on whatever screen they wish.

title: Binge viewing changes how series are written
description: Binge-watching (many episodes in a row) is older than streaming, but autoplay made it effortless, and writers began shaping seasons as one long story.

facts.text: To binge-watch is to watch many or all episodes of a TV series in rapid succession.
Binge viewing predates Netflix: cable networks aired marathons of classic shows in the late 1990s, and binging became routine with TV on DVD a decade later.
On Netflix, the next episode of a series queues up automatically as soon as the previous one ends.
Broadcast TV writers build peril at the end of each act to keep viewers watching through commercial breaks.
Writer Marc Bernardin notes that binge viewers skip the 'previously on' recap and that writers describe a streaming season as 'breaking a 10-hour movie'.

title: Newton Minow's 'vast wasteland'
description: In 1961 FCC chairman Newton Minow called commercial TV a vast wasteland, pushed the networks toward longer news and won the first federal money for educational TV.

facts.text: In May 1961, FCC chairman Newton Minow, appointed by President Kennedy, told the National Association of Broadcasters that commercial television was a 'vast wasteland' and argued for public service television.
Minow encouraged the commercial networks to expand their nightly news from 15 minutes to half an hour.
Minow pushed through the Educational Television Facilities Act of 1962, the first federal funds for educational TV, a step that led five years later to the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967.

title: New Hollywood: directors take control
description: From the late 1960s, surprise hits, television and foreign films pushed Hollywood toward young, film-school-trained directors, until blockbusters and costly flops swung control back to the studios.

facts.text: New Hollywood ran roughly from the mid-1960s to the early 1980s and began with surprise hits such as Bonnie and Clyde (1967), The Graduate (1967) and Easy Rider (1969).
Audiences were increasingly drawn to television, and many were drawn to innovative foreign films such as the French New Wave, Italian Neorealism and Kurosawa Akira's work.
In the early 1970s a younger cohort nicknamed the movie brats, including Coppola, Lucas, Scorsese and Spielberg, often came to Hollywood through newly established film schools.
Britannica describes New Hollywood films as a decisive rejection of the old studio system in favor of director-driven creativity and experimentation.
After the massive success of Jaws (1975), studios began prioritizing potential blockbusters and steering away from experimental, director-driven projects.
Michael Cimino's Heaven's Gate (1980) went nearly four times over an already huge budget, was proportionately one of the biggest failures in movie history and was a disaster for United Artists.
Heaven's Gate was an epic Western, and its failure ended most studios' interest in reviving the Western genre.

title: Bonnie and Clyde borrows from the French New Wave
description: Bonnie and Clyde's writers wanted Truffaut or Godard to direct it, and the film's editing drew on their work.

facts.text: Bonnie and Clyde (1967), directed by Arthur Penn, tore down barriers in the screen depiction of violence and sexuality.
Screenwriters David Newman and Robert Benton loved the work of Truffaut and Godard; Truffaut, their first choice to direct, passed, and Godard also declined.
Bonnie and Clyde's sensational final sequence was created with editing techniques inspired by the work of Jean-Luc Godard and François Truffaut.

title: Jaws makes summer the blockbuster season
description: Summer had been the season for lesser films until Jaws in 1975 became the first summer blockbuster and set the marketing pattern that followed.

facts.text: Jaws, Steven Spielberg's Universal film of Peter Benchley's 1974 novel, was first released on June 20, 1975.
Before Jaws, summer releases were typically reserved for lesser films, because audiences then tended to avoid going to the movies in summer.
Jaws is considered the first summer blockbuster; its marketing tactics became the standard for summer blockbusters and changed how Hollywood marketed and distributed films.

title: Jaws opens everywhere at once
description: Instead of opening city by city, Jaws opened in more than 400 US theaters at once, backed by television trailers.

facts.text: Before Jaws, films typically opened first in a major city, then debuted in other cities and towns over the course of several weeks.
Jaws opened in more than 400 theaters across the United States on its first weekend.
In the week before its release, Jaws was heavily promoted on television with 30-second trailers.

title: The Betamax case
description: Universal sued Sony over home recording; in 1984 the Supreme Court held that selling VCRs was not contributory infringement and that time-shifting was fair use.

facts.text: Movie studios at first resisted the VCR, as they had resisted television some three decades earlier.
Universal City Studios sued Sony, arguing that because Betamax owners recorded its copyrighted TV programs, Sony was liable for their infringement.
On January 17, 1984, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4, in an opinion by Justice John Paul Stevens, that selling VCRs to the public was not contributory infringement.
The Court held that recording a broadcast to watch later at home, called time-shifting, was fair use, and that copying equipment may be sold if capable of substantial noninfringing uses.

title: Rentals become part of a film's income
description: Expensive tapes made renting the norm, and by the mid-1980s rentals were a significant share of what a film earned.

facts.text: In the early 1980s, prerecorded tapes often cost $100 or more, so most people paid around five dollars to rent a video, sometimes with a player, for a night or a few days.
By 1983 most studios had stopped trying to license their films on video and began selling tapes to rental stores and home users.
Video rentals soon made up a significant share of a film's total revenue, and Hollywood began planning for rental income when setting film budgets.

title: Independent film: made outside the studios
description: An independent film is made outside the major studio system; with little money, Cassavetes and Romero found new ways to work.

facts.text: Independent film refers to films produced outside the major film studio system.
John Cassavetes financed his first film as director, Shadows, partly with donations sent after he appealed for money on a radio program.
Shadows was shot on 16-mm film over about two and a half years and was semi-improvised.
Shadows (1959) is generally acknowledged to have inaugurated the American independent filmmaking movement.
Cassavetes paid for later films with his acting, which was sought after by the same studios that were reluctant to back his directing.
In 1968 George Romero and several friends pooled their money to make the low-budget Night of the Living Dead, which major studios rejected but which became a cult favorite.
Night of the Living Dead set the pattern for modern zombie movies by separating the monsters from Vodou and using contemporary settings.

title: Sundance: a stage for independent film
description: Begun in 1978 as the Utah/US Film Festival and later run by Redford's Sundance Institute, Sundance became known for launching independent filmmakers.

facts.text: The Sundance Film Festival began in 1978 in Salt Lake City as the Utah/United States Film Festival, came under Robert Redford's Sundance Institute, founded to nurture independent filmmakers, and took the Sundance name in 1991.
Sundance became known for jump-starting the careers of American independent filmmakers, including the Coen brothers, Steven Soderbergh and Quentin Tarantino.

title: Miniatures and forced perspective
description: Scale models are cheap and easy to handle; filmed faster than 24 frames per second and placed near the lens, they can pass for full-size things.

facts.text: Miniatures, or scale models, are often used in special effects because they are relatively inexpensive and easy to handle.
Models may be filmed at more than 24 frames per second, so they play back in slow motion, for more realistic-looking perspective and time scale.
Forced perspective makes objects look larger, smaller, nearer or farther than they are: the closer something is to the camera, the larger it appears.

title: Matte paintings on glass
description: Painters put scenery on glass in front of the camera and filmed the action through the clear parts, a method credited to Norman Dawn in 1907.

facts.text: Matte painting is attributed to filmmaker Norman Dawn, who first used it in his 1907 film Missions of California.
Matte painters painted scenery on glass, leaving parts unpainted; with the glass in front of the camera, actors were filmed through the clear parts.
The distant Emerald City in The Wizard of Oz (1939) is a matte painting, and Gone With the Wind is filled with matte-painted backdrops.

title: Stop motion: one pose per frame
description: Stop-motion animators photograph a model in slightly different positions, one frame at a time, so a second of film can take 24 poses.

facts.text: Stop-motion animation photographs objects in slightly different positions to create the illusion of movement.
If a model is moved for every frame, one second of film at the standard 24 frames per second takes 24 separate poses.
For Jason and the Argonauts (1963), Ray Harryhausen spent four months animating a battle between Jason, two Argonauts and an army of skeletons.

title: King Kong and Willis O'Brien
description: King Kong (1933) turned an 18-inch puppet into a star through Willis O'Brien's stop motion, rear projection and mattes, and inspired Ray Harryhausen.

facts.text: King Kong (1933), directed by Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack, featured pioneering effects by Willis O'Brien, including stop-motion animation.
Kong was mainly an 18-inch (45-cm) puppet designed by O'Brien, supplemented by giant arms, hands and feet for close-ups.
O'Brien combined animated models with live action using miniature rear projection and traveling mattes, which join separately filmed foreground and background.
Britannica calls King Kong the first significant feature film to star an animated character.
After seeing King Kong, Ray Harryhausen began making stop-motion films in his parents' garage, and he later worked with Willis O'Brien.

title: Cel animation
description: Characters inked and painted on clear cels are laid over a painted background and photographed, so only the moving parts are drawn.

facts.text: An animation cel is a line drawing on the face of a transparent sheet of cellulose acetate, colored with paint on the back.
Painted cels were registered in succession over painted backgrounds and photographed on an animation camera stand.
In the cel process, characters drawn on transparent celluloid sheets were laid over painted backgrounds, so only the moving parts had to be drawn.
On December 19, 1914, Earl Hurd applied for a patent on using transparent sheets over a background photographed through them.

title: Snow White: Disney's gamble
description: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), the first full-length animated feature from an American studio, was a costly risk called Disney's Folly that became a hit.

facts.text: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) was the first full-length animated feature film from an American studio.
Snow White was Walt Disney's biggest gamble to date: an expensive production worked on by hundreds of technicians that became known as Disney's Folly.
On release, Snow White was an immediate box-office sensation, and it set the standard for later Disney animated films.

title: How a computer makes a picture
description: Computer animation builds models from polygons, gives them surfaces and light, then generates and renders a sequence of frames.

facts.text: Computer models such as the Utah Teapot are built from many small polygons and can be shown as a wire-frame image.
In Phong shading, each pixel takes into account the surface texture and all light sources, giving more realistic results but slower rendering.
Ray tracing follows imaginary rays of light through a scene using the laws of reflection and refraction, and is computationally expensive.
Once a three-dimensional figure is digitized, a computer can generate a sequence of images that move it through space, and computers can supply in-between frames.

title: Toy Story, the first computer-animated feature
description: Toy Story (1995), made by Pixar with Disney, was the first entirely computer-animated feature: 114,240 rendered frames.

facts.text: Toy Story (1995), directed by John Lasseter and made by Pixar with Disney, was the first entirely computer-animated feature-length film.
Toy Story took 114,240 frames of computer animation and 800,000 machine hours to render.
At 24 frames per second, Toy Story's 114,240 frames make 4,760 seconds, about 79 minutes of film.

title: What digital gave filmmakers
description: Digital cameras took over from the 1990s to the mid-2010s; films now travel as files and can be restored digitally.

facts.text: Digital cinematography, which records images digitally rather than on film, began to take off in the 1990s and had become dominant by the mid-2010s.
In 2018 Martin Scorsese wrote that almost all pictures are shot with digital cameras, and even those shot on film are edited, color-timed and finished digitally.
In theaters, a film is now usually shown from a Digital Cinema Package sent over the internet or on a drive plugged into the projector.
Digital restoration can repair damaged frames, giving old films whole new lives.

title: What film still does better
description: Digital data can vanish unless migrated, and the Academy found no digital format that lasts like film, which advocates also prefer for its look.

facts.text: Digital information sometimes simply disappears, which has happened to more than one major studio picture, so files must be migrated to each new format.
The Academy's 2007 report The Digital Dilemma found no digital archival master format or process with longevity equivalent to film.
Scorsese calls film, now on a strong Mylar base, still the most reliable and durable means of preserving movies.
Many advocates argue that film has far superior visual quality to digital video.

title: Pixar: from a director's company to Toy Story
description: Lucasfilm's computer division (1979) became Pixar (1986) and, through a 1991 Disney deal, made Toy Story: business and technology together.

facts.text: In 1979 Lucasfilm, George Lucas's production company, hired Ed Catmull to lead its new computer division.
In 1986 the computer division was spun off as an independent business, Pixar, controlled by Apple cofounder Steve Jobs.
In 1991 Pixar agreed with Disney to jointly develop, produce and distribute three computer-animated feature films.

title: Mise-en-scène: everything put in front of the camera
description: Mise-en-scène, "putting in the scene", covers setting, props, costume, lighting and where the actors stand; the setting can amplify emotion or mood.

facts.text: Mise-en-scène, "putting in the scene", covers what is placed before the camera: setting and props, costume, lighting, and the actors and their positions.
Décor, the setting and the objects in a scene, can be used to amplify a character's emotion or the dominant mood of a film.
Costume can signify character, advertise fashions, or make clear distinctions between characters.

title: Placement and size in the frame show relationships
description: Where a figure stands and how large it appears can foster intimacy or swallow a character; Citizen Kane places the boy far back in the snow while adults decide his future.

facts.text: Shot scale can foster intimacy with a character or swallow the character in its surroundings; Welles used it in Citizen Kane to show a changing power relationship.
In Citizen Kane, the boy Kane is a small figure playing in the snow at the back of the shot while, indoors, adults arrange for someone else to raise him.

title: Color sets mood, but its meaning depends on the film
description: Filmmakers use color to establish character or emotion, but a color has no fixed meaning: red can mean passion in one film and decay in another.

facts.text: Besides realism or glamour, color is used to create visual patterns and to establish character or emotion.
In Juliet of the Spirits (1965), Fellini's first color feature, colors separate the heroine's everyday bourgeois life from her fantasy daydreams.
Colors carry no fixed meaning: Yale contrasts red as passion in Zhang Yimou's Ju Dou (1990) with red as stagnation and tainted blood in Bergman's Cries and Whispers (1972).

title: Color grading: repainting a film after the shoot
description: O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000) was the first live-action film extensively colour-corrected by computer, turning green Mississippi into a sepia past.

facts.text: O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000) was the first live-action film extensively colour-corrected, or graded, by computer; the Coens wanted a sepia, old-timey look.
Its Mississippi locations were far too green, so cinematographer Roger Deakins spent a reported 11 weeks adjusting the digital image, yellowing it.

title: Pace: how long each shot lasts sets your pulse
description: Editing sets a fast or slow rhythm that shapes mood, and holding a shot can matter as much as cutting it.

facts.text: Editing shapes a film's sense of time by setting a fast or slow rhythm, and rhythm contributes decisively to its mood.
Deciding to extend a shot can be as significant as deciding to cut it; a long take can feel tense and spellbinding, or flowing and carefree.

title: What the edit holds back
description: Leaving something out of the frame, offscreen, is a common way to build suspense.

facts.text: Offscreen space, part of the story world that the frame does not show, is commonly used to build suspense in horror films and thrillers.

title: A score steers how you read a scene
description: In Boltz's study, the same ambiguous clips read differently, and were remembered differently, with positive, negative or no music.

facts.text: In Marilyn Boltz's 2001 study, viewers watched three ambiguous film clips with positive music, negative music or none, then predicted the ending and judged the characters.
Compared with no music, positive and negative music biased viewers' interpretations, and their later memories of the film, toward the music's mood.
Boltz concluded that music supplies a framework for reading characters and their motives, and guides attention, shaping which details are remembered or misremembered.

title: Expository, observational and participatory documentaries
description: Bill Nichols sorted documentaries into modes: expository films argue through narration, observational films watch quietly, participatory films put the filmmaker in the scene.

facts.text: In Introduction to Documentary (2001), Bill Nichols identified six modes of documentary; one mode usually dominates a film, but a film can mix them.
Expository documentaries argue a point through authoritative 'voice-of-God' narration, using images as evidence; Grierson's Night Mail (1936) is an example.
Observational documentaries use an unobtrusive camera with minimal intervention and no narration or interviews, as in D. A. Pennebaker's Don't Look Back (1967).
In participatory documentaries the filmmaker appears on camera and interviews people, admitting that their presence shapes events, as in Michael Moore's Roger & Me (1989).
Britannica sums up the difference: direct cinema observed like a fly on the wall, while cinéma vérité participated like a fly in the soup.

title: Shaping the truth without inventing it
description: Grierson called documentary the creative treatment of actuality: framing, sets, editing, music and reenactment shape it, and The Thin Blue Line shows staging used honestly.

facts.text: Documentary pioneer John Grierson described documentaries as creative treatment of actuality.
Night Mail (1936) intercut real footage of the mail train with scenes shot on elaborate studio sets.
Errol Morris's The Thin Blue Line (1988) reviewed the case of Randall Dale Adams, on death row for killing a Texas police officer, and argued he was innocent.
Morris's staged scenes do not show what he believed happened; they show each witness's conflicting account so viewers can grasp each one.
Philip Glass's score often plays under the interviews, adding an emotional inflection to the testimony.
The film played a major role in Adams's release from prison the following year, 1989.

title: Adaptation: showing, cutting and changing a book
description: A film must show what a book tells and fit it into a running time: the 1939 Wizard of Oz turned silver shoes ruby for color and made Oz a dream.

facts.text: Dorothy's shoes are silver in L. Frank Baum's book; for the 1939 film they became ruby, reportedly to take full advantage of color photography.
Screenwriter Noel Langley came up with ruby, probably because red would stand out against the yellow brick road.
In a departure from Baum's book, the film makes Dorothy's trip to Oz a dream, with Kansas scenes in sepia-toned black and white and Oz in Technicolor.

title: The auteur theory: the director as author
description: The auteur theory, from French critics around Cahiers du cinéma and named in English by Andrew Sarris, treats the director as a film's author.

facts.text: The auteur theory sees the director, who oversees every sound and image, as a film's major creative force, more its author than the screenwriter.
The idea grew in France in the late 1940s and was advanced through the magazine Cahiers du cinéma, founded in 1951.
American critic Andrew Sarris brought the idea to the US, calling it the auteur theory in his 1962 essay 'Notes on the Auteur Theory in 1962'.

title: The case for film as a team effort
description: Pauline Kael's 'Raising Kane' credited Citizen Kane's co-writer, and Toland advised Welles on camera and light: evidence that films have many authors.

facts.text: In 'Raising Kane' (1971), critic Pauline Kael challenged Welles's role as Citizen Kane's auteur and named co-writer Herman J. Mankiewicz its main creative force.
Sarris and Peter Bogdanovich were among Kael's notable opponents, questioning both her argument and her facts.
Welles later admitted that his cinematographer, Gregg Toland, advised him on lighting effects and camera placement.

title: A method for watching closely
description: Watch once to experience the film, again with timestamped notes; name the choices (angles, light, sets, sound, costume, editing), then ask how they shape your understanding.

facts.text: It helps to watch a film once straight through without notes, experiencing it as intended, then a second time for analysis and notes.
Taking notes with timestamps on the second viewing lets you track what you noticed and when, and find scenes again.
Film analysis goes beyond the story to choices such as camera angles, lighting, set design, sound, costume and editing.
Then ask how the choices you noticed shape your understanding: if one person is always shot from a low angle, what does that say about their role?
